maintopic: CANADA-AUSTRALIA    ANNOUNCEMENT OF SIGNING OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that today in Canberra representatives of the governments of Canada and Australia signed a new trade agreement between the two countries. It is the Canadian government's intention to seek parliamentary approval of the new agreement at the present session of parliament and a bill to this effect is now being prepared.
In the meantime I am tabling the agreement so that hon. members will be aware of its terms. Additional copies are available for members upon request. The agreement will come into force when ratified by both governments.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an announcement to make with regard to the 1958-59 wheat, oats and barley pools. The Canadian wheat board has substituted a report dealing with the financial position of this account-that is, the 1958-59 wheat account-and indicates it to be in a surplus position. The board has advised that it is possible to make an interim payment to producers of 10 cents per bushel on all grades of wheat delivered to the 1958-59 pool, and the government has approved this interim payment.
Producers delivered a total of 366,989,780 bushels to the 1958-59 wheat pool. The interim payment will involve tb* distribution of $36,698,978. The board will be in a position to start issuing interim payment cheques in about three weeks time.
The wheat board has submitted a statement in regard to the financial position of the oats and barley pool accounts. The board reports that selling operations are well advanced and that the two pools can be closed in the near future. Therefore when the interim wheat payment has been completed there will be a distribution of the final surpluses in the 1958-59 oats and barley pools.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We are now on supplementary estimates and considering an estimate dealing with a matter that we have not had an opportunity to discuss since the estimates were tabled at the last session of parliament. On the point of order, during the question period earlier this day when questions were being directed to the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Labour about this problem, the Speaker made the observation that in a few minutes the house would be in committee to discuss the estimates of the Department of Labour, and at that time the unemployment situation could be discussed.
Tha Chairman: That is true.

I wish to add something, but I thought my colleague in other matters, the Minister of Finance, wanted to say something on this point. Before you make a ruling, sir, I must join v/ith the hon. member for Laurier and others in asking you to give very careful consideration to a ruling which, if pursued in the vein suggested, would in my opinion violate one of the most important privileges of members of the house. There is no limitation on the discussion of the problem of unemployment on an item in the estimates; otherwise we might as well close this place up.
Let me give you an example of the consequences of what Your Honour is suggesting. On the orders of the day today the hon. member for Laurier initiated some questions to the Minister of Transport with regard to lay-offs on the Canadian National Railways. I would, however, put my argument on a much broader base than that. We are discussing, it is true, the winter works program. How could we discuss the adequacy of that program unless we could relate it to the fact that some 774,000 people in this country, on the authority of the minister, are looking for work? I suggest to you that we cannot discuss this winter works program unless we can determine its adequacy or inadequacy in the light of the problem that exists.
For instance, last week we had from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate a constructive proposal in which he suggested to the Minister of Labour that in addition to this program, as a means of putting people to work, the government should accelerate its vocational training program. I suggest to you therefore, Mr. Chairman, with much respect that having in mind what the Speaker said on the orders of the day today, having in mind what has always been the practice of this house, in a matter of this importance the rules should be interpreted as they have always been interpreted, to allow the fullest discussion on unemployment or employment in relation to this particular program. I suggest to you that any other interpretation would be contrary to the letter and the spirit of proper debate in this house.

speechtext: I wish to comment very briefly on the point of order, because the hon. member for Laurier put forward a proposition for which I think there is no justification. speechtext: That is the point with which, respectfully, I must disagree. I think the point of order raised by the minister is well taken. We are discussing here payments to Indian bands and to municipalities, but we are not discussing other aspects of the program or the importance of them to labour during the wintertime. As I said on this point, hon. members will have an opportunity to discuss this "do it now" program, but we are now
Supply-Labour
concerned only with the contribution of the 50 per cent of the payroll costs of certain projects by the municipalities.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I be allowed to raise just one point which I think perhaps has escaped the attention of the committee?
Is it a point of order?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, it is a point of order. As I say, it is a point which I think has escaped the attention of the committeee. The hon. member is attempting to refer to and discuss the "do it now program" as it is applied. What I want to bring to your attention, Mr. Chairman, is this. The vote now under consideration and discussion is an incentive program. The item reads in part as follows:
Payments to provinces in respect of Indian bands under the municipal winter works incentive program during the 1959-60 and 1960-61 fiscal years-
It would strike me that anything that indicates an incentive to works during the winter surely could not be inadmissible in such a discussion, and that is all the hon. member is trying to do.

It is not my intention, in raising a point of order, to curb discussion or try to direct Your Honour in what you are trying to do by way of interpreting the rules. However, I wish to point out, in response to what the hon. member for Laurier has said, that in the regular estimates of the Department of Labour there is an item which has to do with the do it now winter works program. It is a separate item.
May I be heard on the point of order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member for Assiniboia would be satisfied to read his telegram and then make his argument I think we might as well let him finish the reading of his telegram. If he will be satisfied to read it and then come back to the discussion I would hold that he can finish the reading of the telegram.

Mr. Chairman, you have now been much more lenient with me than required by any request I had in mind. I felt that the first sentence of this telegram which I have already read was in order on the basis of your prior ruling. In keeping with the importance of this situation I think I would not be doing my duty if I did not read the whole telegram. Since you have invited me to read the whole of the telegram I shall do that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member on reading this telegram will produce an argument which is relevant. I hope he will not disappoint me.

Supply-Labour
Mr. Chairman, you have invited me to read the telegram and I accept your invitation. I hope I will have an opportunity of concluding the telegram before a point of order is raised on it.
Read the telegram.

The telegram is from L. K. Abbott, general chairman of the Atlantic region, brotherhood of railway, transport and general workers. It is addressed to me at the House of Commons and is as follows:
The do it now campaign originated Moncton with C.N.R. one of main participants but immediately afterwards C.N.R. orders mass lay-off of workers many of whom being members of Canadian brotherhood of railway transport and general workers. Also C.N.R. press release by Moncton vice president glorifyingly advocates optimistic outlook for 1960 in maritimes. Laid off men will find it impossible obtain other work. Our organization strongly protests action C.N.R. and enlists your immediate support to cancel C.N.R. top level instructions reduce forces and direct return to work our laid off members.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think there is any doubt that detailed reference to the management of the C.N.R. is not in order under discussion of this item, but it was my opinion, and I think it is correct in the light of your ruling, that it was in order to point out the general situation in Moncton, particularly in the light of a meeting which had been held in that city in order to get winter works projects under way, in order to get do it now winter works projects under way, to deal with this very difficult situation. As has been already pointed out in the discussion of the government's answer to the unemployment situation at this time, there is the huge total of 774,000 Canadians who are applying for work. This is a very serious unemployment situation in my opinion, and no matter which set of figures may be taken I feel that the government's response to this unemployment situation is most inadequate.
During the discussion the minister has given us the information that during last year 32,000 people obtained work on site as a result of this program. The program is being increased this year, but it is certainly not going to result in anything like a full employment program. What bothers me is the apparent feeling in the government that it has provided, and is providing, a solution to the very difficult unemployment problem across this country.
I say to the minister with great respect that the action which is proposed, the $15 million estimate which is under discussion, is no answer whatsoever to what is in fact a very serious, grave and growing unemployment problem. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the minister himself is not fulfilling the duty of a responsible minister in the government
[The Chairman.]
of Canada in the attitude he himself is taking at this time with regard to unemployment. The attitude of the minister is this, that this is not a bad situation and things are reasonably good.
How can you tell?

By his own statement and the answer of the government now, by bringing in what is a very moderate estimate, compared with a total estimate of $6,000 million, of $15 million to pay half the labour cost in a very restricted policy to deal with unemployment. At page 511 of Hansard of this session the minister said there was evidence that the recession has been overcome, and that the measures taken by this government have been effective.
I was quoting the Canadian Labour Congress.
Oh, no.
Further on.
Oh, no; the minister is very much in error. If he looks at page 511 he will see that they were the statements of the minister himself.
I was paraphrasing the Canadian Labour Congress.

Not at all. The minister referred to the hon. member for Essex East. Let me read the full sentence:
If the hon. member has shown perhaps a lessened tendency towards doom and despair this session I think his change of heart is understandable in view of the evidence that the recession has been overcome and that the measures taken by this government have been effective.

For the information of the hon. member may I just refer him to what the Canadian Labour Congress say on page 14 of their brief; that the government took certain measures which helped to lift us out of the recession. That is the statement of the Canadian Labour Congress. Does the hon. member deny that is true?
If the minister was fair he would read their statement with regard to unemployment in full. They have viewed this as a very serious situation.
That is a complete sentence quoted from the Canadian Labour Congress.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I think we are
straying again from the item under discussion, and a general debate on unemployment is developing. I would ask the hon. member for Assiniboia, as well as the minister who is replying, to stick to the item under discussion.

Mr. Chairman, all I was saying when the minister interrupted was that the minister feels that the recession is over and that this item in the estimates is adequate to deal with the unemployment which is prevalent today in this country.

I suppose the hon. member
disagrees with the Canadian Labour Congress?

I am not disagreeing with
the statement they made that certain measures helped-helped-lift us out of the recession. But we are still in a recession.
No one is denying that.

Ask the three quarters of a
million Canadians who are applying for jobs whether we are in a recession, and I think the answer will be that we are in a recession. I take issue with the statement the minister made, which is not the statement of the Canadian Labour Congress; because he quoted a paragraph from the Canadian Labour Congress after he made his own statement. I dispute and disagree with the statement the minister has made that the recession has been overcome. The recession is not overcome. We are in a recession that has demanded at least this much, namely a very adequate winter works program that will be of some benefit to the people of this country.
I think unemployment in Canada is serious, and exceedingly serious for the three quarters of a million Canadians who have applied for jobs. I think it is serious if you ask the families of unemployed workers how they can live on payments of around $33 a week.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I am sure the
hon. member does not wish to disagree with the Chair. I have said before that references may be made to unemployment but it is not the subject of the item under discussion. If the hon. member wishes to discuss the program, or to say it is not sufficient, that it should be otherwise or that it does not cure unemployment, very well; but to discuss unemployment generally as he has for the last few minutes is completely out of order.

Mr. Chairman, with great
respect, the other evening you allowed the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to make some general remarks of some 30 minutes' duration on the question of the the government's policy toward unemployment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I raised a point
of order when the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was speaking. I said that if some remarks relating to unemployment
Supply-Labour
were introductory I would not object. I suggest that the hon. member for Assiniboia should read Hansard and he will find that afterwards the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate discussed the program primarily in relation to Newfoundland.

I thought the hon. gentleman
spent most of his time quoting past statements of the government, but the record will show whether or not the hon. gentleman was strictly in order in line with the interpretation Your Honour is now making as to the rules.
I suggest that the minister does not think the unemployment situation is serious when he has brought in an estimate which may result in the placing of 45,000 people or so in employment at a time when approximately 754,000 have applied for jobs. This program that is now before us is not an answer to the unemployment situation. It means there will be further suffering among the unemployed in Canada. It means that the government is prepared to allow an unemployment rate of between 5 per cent and 12 per cent, when some years ago economists were telling us that full employment meant not more than 2 per cent out of work.
The government could do much more than it has done. It held a conference in the summer of 1958 at which the winter work program was discussed. As a result of that conference and the action taken we had the program of a year ago. The minister did not take the position that there was any necessity for a program for the next year. He considered it a temporary measure. He said that in his opinion the program that was in effect met the situation, and he was not sure that they would need another. The government has now brought in the same program, and in my opinion it is most inadequate to meet the present situation.
I have a number of suggestions I should like to make to the minister. The first is that the percentage contribution by the federal government should be increased from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. That would be a good thing to stimulate employment. This is borne out by the fact that some provinces have themselves added 25 per cent to the payments made under this program. This proposal would result in greater employment and greater use of the winter work program. In his introductory statement the minister pointed out that the payment by the federal government covers only some 12 per cent or 13 per cent of the cost of the works projects undertaken through this scheme. I invite the minister to consider the interest rate municipalities have to pay to obtain money to qualify for participation in the program.

Supply-Labour
As a second proposal I suggest that the government should activate the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, which was passed in 1938. It has been of limited use, but has not been used at all for years. It is a good act, and the unemployment situation prevalent in Canada today in my opinion requires that the act be used. This is the type of act that could be used to cover the projects contemplated by this resolution. One of the difficulties municipalities have in co-operating with the government under this program is, of course, the need to find revenues to pay their share of the wage cost, as well as the greater part of the cost which arises apart from the wages that are involved.
Section 4 of the act to which I referred provides for money to be supplied on a loan basis to municipalities at a rate of 2 per cent per annum. The unemployment situation is of such an emergency character that the government should proceed with the reactivation of this legislation. It is already on the statute books, and the only thing required to make it operative is an item in the estimates.
As a third proposal I urge the minister and his department to be more active in arranging with the municipalities a shelf of works projects that would be readily available in times of unemployment. If such a shelf were available then works projects could be undertaken when emergencies arise. Unemployment insurance is an excellent thing, but it is no substitute for jobs. The old' concept of some 20 years ago, that there should always be available a shelf of public works which would provide full employment oportunities, is a concept that should commend itself to the government.
There are several suggestions I should like to make that are more in the field of the general economic policies of the government. The government should take steps to increase the consumption of goods. Steps should ibe undertaken to increase the incomes of the low income groups. Steps should be taken of an international nature to stimulate Canadian production and exports.
I wish to underline once again the relief of members of this party that this country faces a grave unemployment emergency at this time. The measure now before us, although welcome and helpful, is inadequate by itself to deal with this situation. Specific steps should be taken to improve the operation of a program like this by increasing the federal government's contribution from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. The government should bring into operation the long-neglected Municipal Improvements Assistance Act.

If the government would follow these suggestions and institute other economic measures, I am certain that at some future date the minister's statement that Canada is out of the recession would be accurate.

Mr. Chairman, before the hon. member sits down I wonder if he would permit a question. I listened very carefully to his remarks. The hon. member admitted in his own words that we are out of the recession because of certain actions taken by this government. In the same breath he said we are still in the recession. How can the hon. member stay on both sides of the fence? I wonder if he would care to reconcile those two statements?
I did not use those words. I was quoting.
But the hon. member agreed with those words.

I should very much like to have the opportunity of replying to the hon. gentleman's well considered and highly important question, as to whether or not in one breath I said we were out of the recession and in the next said we were still in the recession. The Minister of Labour had quoted the one sentence from the brief of the Canadian Labour Congress. I requoted that. To answer my hon. friend's question very definitely, I tell him that in my opinion we are still in a recession.
Do you agree with the Canadian Labour Congress?

Would the minister care to comment on the request by certain boards of education that some work being done by those boards be allowed under the winter works program? The claim is that some jobs can be done in the wintertime that would provide work for people who are unemployed and are not able to perform the work now permissible under the plan.

This matter has been brought up and considered on previous occasions in regard to last winter's works program and also this one. At the moment the decision is that boards of education could not be included in this program, since we include only works undertaken by municipalities.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Skeena made the remark some time ago that he thought the discussion here was deplorable, and that in his opinion the government and the official opposition were playing politics with this very important question. Actually it is too bad that he is not in his seat just now, because he would find that

many constructive suggestions are being made to the government to improve this inadequate measure.
I will try to confine myself to the question under discussion, but I find it very difficult to deal with such an important question without at some time or other referring to unemployment and even giving examples which may not be general in Canada. I deplore the fact that the minister has severed his civic connections. If he were still mayor of the important municipality he represents I am sure he would have submitted to this government a winter works program and a policy which would be much better than the one that has been presented to us.

I do not like to interrupt the hon. member, but would he not agree with this? First of all, I thank the hon. member for his kind words, but would he not agree that a step in the right direction has been taken in the submission of a plan, even though he may not agree with me that it is as full in scope as it could be?
Any definite step taken to improve working conditions in Canada by a winter works program certainly is a step in the right direction. The only thing is that the minister took too short a step.
It is better than no step.

The program as submitted by the Minister of Labour is entirely inadequate. Further, a program of winter works should be a program covering a period of two years. It is my opinion, and it is the opinion of most of the administrators of Canadian municipalities, that the program of this government does not cover the needs of the municipalities sufficiently to make it a workable and good program. While it covers 50 per cent of the labour cost, it does not do anything to cover a part of the material cost or a part of the machine rental and maintenance cost which it should include if it is going to be profitable to municipalities.
Another thing I find is that the Department of Labour, through the minister, presented the program to this house for a period of time that is too limited. The program now starts on December 1 and runs to May 1. I am sure the Minister of Labour did not take into consideration the time it takes to calculate and design the projects which are to be done by the municipalities. If the municipalities were advised in December-
It runs to April 30.

I did not give the date; I said it was from December to April. I agree with the minister that April 30 should be included in my remarks. Actually, Mr. Chairman, it is impossible for municipalities to gamble in
Supply-Labour
preparing the necessary engineering designs and calculations for winter works they are going to undertake unless they are advised in plenty of time. Unfortunately the minister did not advise the municipalities until September, 1959 that it was his intention again to submit to this house a winter works program or an appropriation to cover it.
There are no complaints about that.
There may not be any complaints on the part of the minister but I am speaking-
From the municipalities.
-of the people who disagree with the minister.
The hon. member is the only one who has disagreed about this so far.
Oh? Nobody is satisfied.

Before I became a member of this house the government constantly accused the Liberal party of not having its ear to the ground. I hope the present minister is not guilty of the same thing of which he accused the Liberals.
I am now speaking for the people whom I meet every day:	I am speaking for the
municipalities with whom I have something to do every day. They realize-and I am sure the minister himself must have heard it at some time or other-that it is impossible, in an economical manner, to prepare winter works programs when they are advised by the minister's office on September 3. It is too far away. When the advice comes on September 3 it puts the municipalities in the position of gambling. If they commenced to work on this program before they were advised that the government was going to proceed with it this year they would be gambling in preparing the engineering works necessary for the program without knowing whether or not the government would decide to legislate so the winter works program could be carried out.
Because the minister comes from the western part of the province I am sure he does not realize that in most places in Canada-
The central part.

The central part; I stand corrected. Because the minister comes from the central part of Ontario I am sure he does not realize, or did not think of it because of his numerous duties in dealing with the great number of unemployed in Canada, that there is a very deep frost penetration in most sections of Canada, and that many of the works programs which are listed in the government's policy are impossible to carry out

Supply-Labour
in the wintertime. For instance, if you are going to lay water mains in the winter you find that the cost increases by about 30 per cent. The government's contribution is 50 per cent of the labour cost. I will prove a little later on that it becomes absolutely uneconomical for municipalities to do anything about laying water mains in the winter.
There is another problem when you do that kind of work in the winter. The work done in the winter causes the roads to deteriorate to a much greater extent in the spring than they would if the work was done in the summer. The problem of re-establishing the roads to their original condition increases the cost considerably. The conditions as proposed by the government in the winter works program, so far as the municipalities are concerned, are entirely unrealistic.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, while the program might make some kind of contribution, it should be submitted to the municipalities in March or April so the necessary preparation could be made and the economies effected at the time they should be. Actually there is no reason why the government did not submit the program much earlier in the year, because it was evident at that time that during the winter there would be a great deal of unemployment. I say this even though the minister did state in the third paragraph of a letter to the premier dated September 3, 1959-which his office supplied to me, incidentally-
We expect the unemployment situation generally to be improved compared with last winter.
If the minister will check on the number of unemployed we had at this time last winter and the number we have now he will find that not only has the condition not improved but that it has deteriorated.
As a matter of information, is the hon. member saying that is a national condition, or is he referring to a particular local area?
From the figures submitted to the house by the minister I would say that this is a national condition.
I suggest that the hon. member do a little travelling and find out.
There is unemployment right in Edmonton, in your own constituency.
You were in office from 1935, and you did not do anything at all.

I will accept the hon. member's suggestion that I probably should do a little more research, but the conditions right now are so evident that not a great deal of research is necessary. Actually the provinces

were only advised on September 9 that the Minister of Labour had decided that this winter there would be some contribution by the federal government toward a winter works program. The provinces took at least the same length of time or maybe longer to advise the municipalities that there was going to be a winter works program. If the minister had waited a couple of weeks more to advise the provinces, and if the provinces had taken a little longer to advise the municipalities, it would have been spring; because spring always comes after winter.
In my opinion the present winter works program submitted by the minister is inadequate and is far too narrow in scope. There is no question but that this can be proven easily; and in that regard I am going to refer to some of the conditions that affect the people of Canada most, but I am not going to read all of them. One condition is that the money will be applied to the construction and major improvement of municipal roads, streets, sidewalks, bridges and underpasses. You do not need to be an expert, Mr. Chairman, to know that when there is 70 to 72 inches of snow on the ground and frost penetration of from five to six feet, the construction and major improvement of municipal roads, streets and sidewalks is impossible. I guess that condition was put in the agreement so it would look important, and so there would be enough conditions to make up a four or five page letter. Otherwise I see no use for it.
Another condition covers the construction and major improvement of municipal water, sewage and storm sewer facilities, not including buildings. If you are constructing a sewer and it is necessary to build a pumping station for the sewer system, the pumping station will not come under the grant from the federal government although it may constitute a very big part of the cost of constructing the sewer project.
Then there is the construction and development of municipal parks and playgrounds, but not including playgrounds that may be attached to schools. I understand that, because playgrounds attached to schools should be and are the responsibility of the department of education. But I am wondering what the minister had in mind in including this provision for the spending of money and time in the winter on the construction or improvement of municipal parks and playgrounds. I am sure the minister did not have in mind that he wanted to provide for more seats in more parks so the increasing number of unemployed would at least be able to sit in comfort. I am sure he did not have that in mind, but as in the case of the construction of

sewers it is not very easy to carry on work when there is frost penetration and a great deal of snow.
I am trying to prove that in the end this program will have cost the dominion government very little, the municipalities will not have benefited from it, and the unemployed will have benefited the least. The bulk of the people required for these projects are secured through the unemployment insurance offices. Actually, as the minister knows, most of the work is done by machinery, but this program covers labour costs only. There is a provision that if skilled men are used, men of the type who are used in that kind of construction, then there must also be a labourer hired for each one of them. To me that sounds like the Petrillo system of having stand-ins for musicians. If you require a man trained to operate a steam shovel and you cannot find in the regular labour force a man who can operate a steam shovel, then you must have a stand-in for him because in order to obtain the grant there must be one employee secured through the unemployment insurance offices for each such man.
Mind you, I do not disagree with that, but there is also a condition that the project must be submitted to the provincial government as well as to the federal government before the job can be started, and in my opinion that is one of the reasons why advising the municipalities at a very late date makes it practically impossible for them to do things in an economic manner.
You realize, Mr. Chairman, that most of these jobs are carried out by municipalities through the issue of debentures, and while this may not have anything to do with the present winter works program or with the unemployed as such, it creates a complication for the municipalities in preparing their programs. It is also stated in the agreement that the municipalities are not to start work before they get the approval of both the provincial and federal governments.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, we were talking about the winter works program and so that hon. members will be able to follow the trend of the discussion on this subject this morning may I be permitted to read an editorial which appeared in the Citizen of December 10, 1958. I shall only read part of it in order to save the time of the committee, but if some members feel something has been eliminated that is important I shall be glad to read the whole editorial.
Supply-Labour
The municipalities, which are contributing 25 per cent of the labour cost of the winter work program, are being asked to undertake projects for which there may be no urgency. At the same time, routine municipal works which have to get under way soon will evidently not be given extra help under the federal winter works program. In these circumstances, the likelihood is that municipalities will draw up a minimum program-
A little lower down in the editorial I read that the acting mayor of an important municipality is reported to have said certain things, and I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, he did say them. This acting mayor, it is reported: -noted the other day, it looks as if the federal winter works program is "a lot of political talk." If it is a bluff, it is one of the most callous ever perpetrated on the Canadian people.
At this time there were between 3,000 and 4,000 people unemployed in the municipality, and this program would be far from adequate to cover the requirements.
From calculations made and the admission of the minister it would appear that out of
800,000	unemployed, only about 34,000 can benefit from the winter works program. Some time ago I had cause to have calculations made on the 1958-1959 winter works program and the situation I found in this municipality was as follows. The municipality to which I am referring had 50 individual projects at an estimated cost of $2,238,803; the estimated subsidy on this was calculated at $164,316. Construction actually took place on 44 of the above mentioned projects with the final cost estimated to be $1,881,629. The subsidy claimed on this program was $156,325, and the subsidy actually received was $141,273.90, and that included the provincial part of the subsidy. This $141,273.90 is actually 7.5 per cent of the estimated total cost of the projects that were completed in that particular season.
If you realize that the provincial government pays a 25 per cent subsidy, then the approximate cost to the federal government was 5.2 per cent of the total construction cost. If you add to this the extra of the high rate of interest on debentures-several years ago it was 4 per cent and it is now 7 per cent- you will realize the cost to the municipality. The last $20 million that the city of Montreal borrowed in the way of debentures cost the city of Montreal 7.58 per cent in interest. If you calculate that the total benefit received by the municipalities from the winter works program is 7.5 per cent, and if you add the cost of high money, namely 7 per cent or more, you will find that the dominion government is actually making no contribution whatever to the municipalities.
Would the hon. member permit a question at this point?

Certainly.

Supply-Labour

Would the hon. gentleman suggest that this program, which it is estimated will enable approximately 40,000 Canadians this year to gain employment, should be dropped because of the high rate of interest to the municipalities?

I think the hon. member should get together with the Minister of Labour because the Minister of Labour said a few days ago in this house that the program would employ between 33,000 and
34,000.	The hon. member has now raised the figure to 40,000, and unless he has had a conference with the minister of which we are not aware, then the figure should remain at 33,000 to 34,000.
Answer my question.

If the hon. member had listened tb me this morning he would have found out that while I am not against the action of the government with regard to the winter works program; I have said it is not complete enough; it does not cover enough and it is not beneficial enough because too many conditions which should be included are left out. Actually, if you figure the cost of the winter works program to a given municipality, the cost of winter work is increased by 12 per cent to 15 per cent. This, as the hon. member will know, has been calculated and it is for that reason most of the municipalities, or a lot of these municipalities, will not apply for the subsidy on the winter works program.
I would have no objection whatever, and I know most municipalities in Canada would not object, if the minister would make his program more inclusive, even if it cost the municipalities a little more. All the municipalities in Canada are anxious, just as the government is and as the opposition is, to eliminate unemployment as it is today. I am sure most municipalities would feel the added expenditure would be warranted if more people benefited from it. As I suggested this morning, I think all municipalities would gratefully receive a program that would include not only a percentage of labour but a percentage of the cost of operation of machines and a percentage of material used.
I read in the newspaper some few days ago that the mayor of Sherbrooke stated that he would not apply for a grant on a winter works program because after a calculation it was found that the program was entirely inadequate and that it did not solve the problem of unemployment in the city of Sherbrooke.
The winter works program as it now stands is a social service cost to the municipalities

even if it does not appear to be so. If it was not for the winter works program, some of the few people that are employed by the municipalities would be drawing their unemployment insurance benefits. It appears to me that this is a method the government is using in order to discharge itself of its obligation of paying unemployment insurance benefits while charging them to the municipalities which benefit very little by it.
In my opinion the program is inadequate because we have, as the Minister of Labour admitted, a great number of unemployed at the present time; and as he has also admitted in this committee, only about 33,000 or 34,000 people benefit by it. With financing at the present high cost of interest, I am afraid that many municipalities will be discouraged in applying for it and what the Minister of Labour intends to accomplish I am afraid will be wasted time and will be of no benefit to anyone. The municipalities are looking to the Department of Labour to review this policy and to make their contribution to the winter works program adequate so that it will be beneficial.
May I request through you, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Labour review the program and accomplish the points that I have raised today. If this was done I am sure every member of this committee would support it unanimously. If this is considered and accomplished, then and only then will the unemployed it is supposed to help to cover benefit from same.
I should like to suggest to the Minister of Labour that some additions are necessary to the present winter works program if it is going to be beneficial. One is that the municipalities should be advised much sooner of the government's intention. Second, it should increase its contribution to include part of the material and machine costs. It should include all cost of a job including the buildings that pertain' to the project that is accepted. It should make the period eligible for grants from November 1 to April 30 instead of the present date. It should also make an announcement early in the spring that this policy will be in effect for a period of two years. If this was done, I feel that what the Minister of Labour intends to do would be accomplished. May I suggest that if the Minister of Labour feels that these conditions are too severe, he inquire among the municipalities in Canada, most of which have exactly the same feeling as I have at the present time.

Last year, Mr. Chairman, although I do not recall the exact date, we in this house received a supplementary estimate, the second supplementary estimate

that was presented to this house; and on page 3 of the supplementary estimates we saw an item pertaining to the winter works program in the amount of $15 million. Today we again have before us a similar supplementary estimate with an identical figure, namely $15 million. This fact would lead one to believe that as far as the minister and the government are concerned, this program which was presented last year and is being presented again this year is an adequate one to meet the situation of unemployment as we have it today in this country.
I listened carefully to the minister the other day. He told us that out of this estimate of $15 million that was passed last year, only about $6| million was used; that is $6J million out of approximately a $50 million program a fact which, by the process of simple arithmetic, shows us that the federal government contributed about 13 per cent to the winter works program of last year. We have this situation in the face of the impression that was created across this country with screaming headlines that here was a federal government prepared to step in on a 50-50 basis to assist the municipalities in meeting the problem of unemployment.
They never said that.
I know it is quite true that they never did say they would pay 50 per cent but they definitely and carefully created that impression throughout the country.
They never did.

Furthermore, again from the minister's report of the other day we find that so far this year the estimate is that the federal government will spend something slightly in excess of $10 million on a program of $84 million, a fact which again by the process of simple arithmetic shows that the federal contribution has dropped from the 13 per cent it was last year down to about 11 per cent this year. Hence in other words they are not even going to do as much this year as they did last year. The minister also mentioned that this was one of the things the government had done and that there were others although he did not elaborate. I should like to mention one or two. When I spoke at some length on this subject last year, as reported at page 1116 of Hansard of February 17, 1959, I said:
This, we find, is the first and only project that this government has put forth designed specifically for the relief of unemployment. They have done other things, such as housing, which has helped but was not designed basically to relieve unemployment.
An hon. member butted in at that point: and he said, "Yes, they were", or in other
Supply-Labour
words that housing was designed basically for the relief of unemployment. But if it was, Mr. Chairman, I wonder why it was abandoned this year. I recall some hon. members who, speaking in the debate last year, painted the rosy picture that the housing program had employed or provided about
400.000	jobs for the people of Canada-I think that was the figure they used-but still we had the anouncement last fall: sorry we are going to have to close up shop because money has run short and we cannot carry on with this program any longer. Possibly that is one of the reasons why we are faced today with the situation in which we have close to 800,000 people looking for work.
Last year, again according to the words of the minister in his report the other day, this winter works program provided about
35.000	jobs. I do not know the duration of those jobs or how long they lasted. Maybe some were for a week, maybe some were a few months. It would probably be difficult to ascertain for just what length of time these jobs were provided. However, we must remember that was only 35,000 out of what we had last year, approximately
600.000	unemployed. 'Based on the same proportion this year, we find that the proposal so far would guarantee approximately 51,000 jobs out of a total of 774,000 unemployed.
I wonder whether the minister and the government really think this program is an answer to this problem. By their own admission-in fact they were quite proud of the thing last year-this was the first time that the federal government had ever taken a step in this field in order actually to try to meet the problem of unemployment. They were quite proud that they were breaking new ground. I do not think they are breaking it very deeply or cultivating it very thoroughly. I remember the situation back in the early thirties. I think it was only in the year 1938 that the unemployment in this country ever exceeded what it is at the present time. I do not think there is any hon. member who would deny that was considered to be the depth of a depression. But today it is no longer a depression; it is not even a recession. The government has told us-we have their word for it-that the recession is over. Now we have seasonal unemployment of 800,000 workers.
We have seen recently a great to-do in our newspapers, on radio and television about the big and much heralded move behind the iron curtain, where the U.S.S.R. is supposed to be sending back something like one and a quarter million troops to civilian life. There is one thing which all these news reports are

Supply-Labour
agreed about and that is that the major reason for this demobilization in Russia is the need of these people in the Russian economy today. They have a shortage of workers, and that is the reason for this move. Now surely, that is something which we should take very carefully into consideration when we think about putting out programs to meet unemployment. How can we afford to have three quarters of a million workers unemployed in this country when countries the size of Russia have to demobilize their forces to fill the jobs which are vacant? How long can we afford the luxury of three quarters of a million unemployed and meet the competition which we have to face from this country? I know-I think we all realize-that there are a lot of employers in this country who believe unemployment is a good thing; that it is a good thing to have a group of men

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member is not following the ruling which I gave this morning. I repeat, there is no objection to discussing unemployment to a certain degree, but I would ask the hon. member to discuss the winter works program as described in the item under discussion. That is the ruling I gave this morning, and I would ask the co-operation of all members on this matter.

I am very sorry, Mr. Chairman; I thought I was relating my remarks very closely to this item.
The other day the minister mentioned in his introductory remarks that this winter works program grew out of a meeting held back in 1958, and was in fact in answer to a request made by the municipalities at the time. He went on to say that the municipalities since that time, through their elected officials and representatives, have made known to the government that they commend very highly this move on the part of the government, and he also went on to say they still do.
I do not know which officials he was talking to, but I will guarantee one thing, and that is that he was not talking to the municipal officials in the area I come from. I recall last year I spoke at some length on this subject and criticized this program quite severely. I found at that time that many of the municipal officials in my area thought I had gone pretty far astray. They said, "After all, it is a little unfair; this is the first time the federal government has made a move in this direction, so what is our member criticizing them for?" But we had a meeting just shortly before this house opened this session at which the municipal council in my town asked me to be present, and the subject of that meeting was the winter works program. They

agreed with every single, solitary thing I had said in the house last year. In fact, they agreed with my remarks to the extent that if the minister checks his files he will find the town of Timmins has this year been unable to implement one single item of the winter works program. It is impossible for them to take advantage of the program.
The hon. member for Russell listed some of the reasons why this was so. He mentioned the climate, the depth of frost, and if the house will pardon the pun, I would say we have far too much "frost" in the province of Ontario. However, he also mentioned the fact that we have sixty to seventy inches of snow. For the information of the house, I think the last count I had of the snowfall in Timmins this year it was something like one hundred and fourteen inches, and the snow is still there because as yet they have not had a single thaw. As I say, there is far too much frost.
How is it possible to do any of the projects within the narrow field of this plan? How is it possible to carry them out under such conditions? As has been pointed out, the federal contribution to the works which were carried out last year amounted to about 13 per cent. I do not know what the provincial contribution was, but I think it is reasonably safe to say that the municipalities had to meet anywhere up to, and in some cases possibly more than, 80 per cent of the cost of these projects. The federal and provincial governments today meet 80 per cent of the cost of relief in the municipalities. They reimburse the municipalities to the tune of 80 per cent of the cost of their relief. In many cases where the municipalities have great difficulty in keeping within their budgets they will look very carefully at the fact that it is much easier to pay 80 per cent of the relief than about 80 per cent of the cost of these projects. I do not think that is the objective that the federal government is aiming at in this program.
There is another point which was touched upon by one or two hon. members, and that is the fact that this program is so designed that the wealthier municipalities can take advantage of it but the poorer municipalities cannot. In addition this year this program has been made available to Indian bands, and the same applies again to them-the wealthier bands can take advantage of it, but the poorer bands cannot.
The right hon. Prime Minister is very good at quoting from the Bible. I would suggest it is very easy to believe that this whole plan has been based upon a quotation from the Bible, whether it came from the Prime Minister or not. I refer to the quotation which

goes something like this: "To them that hath shall be given; but to them that hath not, even that which they hath shall be taken away". I would say that that is certainly the basis of this program under its present terms.
I would like to repeat that this plan is completely worthless, as far as the northern municipalities are concerned, as proved by the fact that the northern municipalities are not taking advantage of it, and cannot. Before it can be implemented by them there are two things which have to be done, even in the present plan, inadequate as it is. First, the length of time has to be stretched out so that it can be used in the months of October and November and in March and April, when the severe weather conditions are not prevailing. Second, the projects themselves have to be broadened out, because in their present form they cannot be used.
Mr. Chairman, as I said at the start, apparently this is the government's only program for the relief of unemployment during the winter months. I would like to point out that according to the figures supplied by the minister himself it will take 22 of these programs to look after the present situation. Surely, Mr. Chairman, this government with all the vision it is supposed to have can come up with a better answer than it has.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few observations on this item. Before doing so, however, I should like to compliment the hon. member for Russell, one who has had a considerable amount of municipal experience, on the contribution he has made here today. I think the Minister of Labour himself who has had considerable experience as the first magistrate in his own city will recognize the value of what was proposed by the hon. member for Russell.
Those of us who have been criticizing this program have done so from a point of view slightly different from that of the hon. member for Russell but I believe what that hon. gentleman has had to say about this program reflects the attitude which, if we can judge from declarations made in the press by municipal leaders, is the opinion which such bodies generally in the country share as to the inadequacy of this program.
No one can claim that a program which puts men to work is on that account not to be supported. Of course, we support this program. Our quarrel is not with the program as such but with its inadequacy in terms of achievement in the year 1958-59 and with what it is calculated to do in 1959-60 on the statements given to the committee by the Minister of Labour the other day and partially again this morning.
Supply-Labour
There can be no doubt about the inadequacy of this program in the face of the serious unemployment problem that now exists in our country. I hope the Minister of Labour will not think that those of us who labour this subject are doing so because of any personal animosity toward him. I believe we ought to try and recognize in these discussions that we have cause to be concerned about a situation that is reflected in the figures which the minister himself has produced. I should be very interested in knowing what the latest situation in terms of the figures which are made available to the minister portends. The last figure he gave us was for January 21. That figure showed that 774,000 persons were seeking work. What the figure was for January 28, I do not know. What the figure for this Friday is, I do not know. It would, I think, be more conducive to the achievement of the business of this committee if the minister would give these figures without being prodded to do so day after day by hon. members of the opposition.
Speaking for myself I should be very happy to relieve the committee of the monotony-if that is what hon. gentlemen wish to call it-of some of the interrogations which are being pursued on this subject day by day. That could be obviated if the minister himself would take the initiative and willingly, without seemingly being compelled, give these figures to the committee. The minister told us that he received them every week. It is true that he altered this statement a few days ago by indicating that he did not receive them every week but his earlier statement confirmed the position he took in that regard last year. In any event, despite what the latest figures are, the fact is that unemployment continues to be serious. We have the right in the face of that situation to test the adequacy of the program which the government put forward.
I asked the Minister of Labour some questions in written form the other day and he gave answers to me on February 3. Those answers may be found at pages 707 and 708 of Hansard. When one looks at those figures surely the minister himself must find it exceedingly difficult to be convinced that this program represents a real achievement by itself. Certainly it is a most unimportant achievement in relation to the problem of unemployment and in relation to the assurances that hon. gentlemen opposite gave to the country as to how they were going to deal with unemployment.
The federal expenditure in 1958-59 is given as $6,452,937.78. Can anyone say that that figure, in the face of the unemployment which existed in this country last year- which totalled 600,000 as of the end of March

Supply-Labour
-represents a real effort to meet unemployment? The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate this morning told us that his province reflected the highest level of unemployment in Canada on a per capita basis.
A Liberal province.
What is Joey doing about it?
My hon. friend said, "What is Joey doing about it?"
It is a national problem.

That remark coming from the hon. gentleman I think indicates that either he does not appreciate or is unsympathetic to the plight of unemployed people in this country. I do not really believe that that is the attitude of the hon. gentleman.
No, it certainly is not.

But just so he will not be misunderstood, I suggest to the hon. member that as these words of his become immortalized once they are uttered in this chamber, if he wishes me to give them the generous interpretation he does, then he should be very careful about his interventions.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Surely, Mr. Chairman.
I again ask the hon. member what is the premier of Newfoundland doing about it?
I am sure the premier of Newfoundland shares-
I asked that question in all seriousness, too.

All right. I am sure the premier of Newfoundland shares the view held by most people in this country and by those who sit on this side of the chamber that the federal government is not living up to its responsibilities in this matter.
I shall go one step further. My hon. friend asked me a question and I will give him the further answer which he deserves because I appreciate that he is sincerely interested in this problem. The premier of Newfoundland, I am sure, would welcome an opportunity of sitting down at a conference with the federal government on this problem. That was one of the suggestions the Minister of Labour himself made when he was sitting in opposition as a means by which this problem could be resolved.
Would the hon. member like to ask another question?

Mr. Chairman, an unidentified hon. member suggested that I ask another question so it seems quite in order that I do so. Has the premier of Newfoundland made any concrete suggestions as to what could be done to relieve the unemployment problem in the province of N ewf oundland?

I shall be glad to indicate some of those suggestions if my hon. friend will just have patience. What I am speaking about now is a proposal that represents one way of dealing with the problem through the calling of a conference of senior levels of government to confer on the matter. That is one of the proposals I made the other day.
We had a conference in July of 1958.

The Minister of Labour never replied to that question but I am asking him now why in 1960 when we have all these people out of work the government does not call a conference with the provinces to try and relieve this problem as hon. members of the government proposed in 1955 should be done.

Mr. Chairman, since the hon. member for Essex East has asked a direct question of me perhaps I may be permitted to bring to his attention the fact that it is quite evident that he has not been too interested in unemployment in Canada or he would have known that such a conference on a much wider basis was called in July of 1958.
How many of the recommendations were implemented?

Well, my hon. friend always comes back to the argument ad hominen. He always says the member for Essex East is obviously not interested in unemployment. I am not going to argue with my hon. friend. My record in public life, in social matters and on these questions, speaks for itself, and I am not dealing with the situation in 1955.

Will the hon. member permit a question? I should like the hon. member for Essex East, in view of what he has just said, to tell the committee how interested he has been in the question of unemployment, particularly in his own constituency, where unemployment has been considerable in the years gone by. During all the time that he sat on the treasury benches since 1935 when, according to the records of this house, did

he ever bring up the situation in Windsor? And what were the suggestions he made to alleviate the situation in his own riding?

I am glad my hon. friend asked that question. He has made the assertion on several occasions when I was not in the house that I had completely disregarded the plight of the unemployed. In the first place-
Will the hon. member permit a question?

Just a minute, now; I am going to answer the minister and I am glad he is here so that I can deal with the question directly. I will not make charges about the hon. gentleman when he is out of the house.
My hon. friend talks about the problems of his constituency. I have a firm belief that representations made by one's constituents are important. The minister does not think that, because I have before me the Oshawa Times of January 5 of this year in which the minister is quoted as follows:
Mr. Starr questioned the worth of letters, "I do not think it makes much difference whether they write letters. We realize their position. It is not necessary to further emphasize it by writing letters", he said. He also indicated that letters in general would not help him much in any issue brought up by his constituents.
That is the view of the minister; it is not my view. It is quite apparent that if the minister did pay attention to representations from his constituents he would not be trying to minimize the severity of this problem, or introduce these irrelevant issues.
When I was a member of the government, of course, my hon. friend knows that as a member of the cabinet I could not rise in my place and take issue with the government of the day.

You had ample opportunity, though.
Mr. " Martin (Essex East): I will let my hon. friend know that I did not hesitate, by the things that I was able to introduce in this house, to show my interest in unemployment.
What were they?
I brought in five different amendments to the old age pensions act; I introduced the disability pensions act.
What about unemployment?

My hon. friend is asking some questions, sir.

You have not answered them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think the exchange between the Minister of Labour and the hon. member for Essex East has helped the discussion to remain strictly relevant. I ask both hon. gentlemen to realize that we are straying away from the item under discussion.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

I am not going to argue, Mr. Chairman, whether or not your objection to this matter is valid; but I point out to you that the Minister of Labour asked me a question. He made a statement and I believe this matter is close enough to relevancy to permit my giving a reply. I will say this to the minister, furthermore. There was no time during the period that I happened to be in the government of Canada when there was the same concern with regard to unemployment as there is now. The record is this:-
You cannot answer.
-during the time-
Seven per cent unemployed.
If my hon. friend thinks he is going to facilitate the passage of these estimates by these boyish, prankish interventions, he is mistaken. I ask him to contain himself.
I thought the Liberal government passed the old age pension act and not the hon. member for Essex East, as he claims.

I ask the minister to address himself to the severity of this problem instead of trying to extricate himself from the difficulty which the extravagant promises of the administration have put him into at the present time.
You must have been a one-man government.

There is my hon. friend again. If he wants to have a debate I will be glad to have a debate with him on this. I will be glad to invite my hon. friend to come to Oshawa, where I am going to speak on March 5, and we will debate this question. I will be glad to invite my hon. friend to come to my own constituency, where we will have a debate and perhaps we can collect enough money to help some of the unemployed.

Supply-Labour

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member for Essex East and the Minister of Labour to come back to the item under discussion.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order; we on this side of the house listened respectfully to a question that was put by the Minister of Labour, and we did not interrupt the minister, not one of us, while he put the question to the hon. member for Essex East. Surely, in all fairness, we are entitled to hear the answer from the hon. member for Essex East without interruptions.
He has no answer.
That is all we ask, and I would not ask anything beyond that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will realize that I have given the hon. member for Essex East the chance to reply.
Not without interruption.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: What I have said applies equally to the Minister of Labour. If the reply of the hon. member for Essex East has to be so lengthy that we have to continue to be out of order for the rest of the afternoon, I do not think we shall make progress. The question was out of order; the hon. member has had occasion to reply and I think the hon. member should realize that the ruling applies to all hon. members.

I am sure we all appreciate your desire to keep order, and I am sure the Minister of Labour and I will do our best to help you in the matter if others in the committee will likewise take a similar course.
I simply want to point out to the Minister of Labour, who is touchy on this matter, that in the 11 years I had the honour and responsibility of serving the government of our country, in seven of those the percentage of unemployment in Canada was under 3 per cent; in two of the four years it was close to 3 per cent; and in the other two years it was close to 4 per cent. Compare those figures with the alarming situation which now confronts our country and one will see the emptiness of the kind of defence to which the minister has resorted.
Let us analyse the expenditure of $6,500,000.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. If the hon. member who has risen wants to put a question about the figures to which the hon. member for Essex East has just referred I would say the question would be out of order because I consider the remarks of the hon. member for

Essex East are out of order in accordance with the ruling I gave this morning. I am sure the hon. member for Essex East would wish to come back to the item under discussion.

I cannot agree with your interpretation of the rules, but because of my argument at the moment, I am prepared to go ahead, since I am dealing directly with the project. However, I would not under any circumstances agree with you, sir, that it was correct to interpret the rules in such a way as to preclude a discussion of the adequacy of this project, this program, in relation to unemployment.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingata -I was about to say this 10 minutes before these excursions were entered into-pointed out that his province was the province that had the highest ratio of unemployment of any province in Canada. Yet in 1958-59, $24,770 was spent by the federal government as its share in this winter works program. Does anyone seriously contend, the Minister of Labour included, that this was really grappling with the problem in that province?
In Ontario, where we had a high number of unemployed in relation to the working force, the total expenditure was $1,999,000. I would put the same question to the Minister of Labour or to any other hon. gentleman. Does anyone suggest that that was vigorously coping with the problem of unemployment?
The minister referred to my own city of Windsor as one of those areas of surplus unemployment which has persisted in that state for a period of over two and a half years. Just look at what has happened with regard to the application of this program in the city of Windsor where there are now some 10,000 applicants for jobs according to the national employment service figures. In 195859 there were five projects in Windsor, and when there were some 10,000 to 12,000 people out of work this program about which the minister boasts so much put 143 people to work for a limited period. Can there be any doubt about the inadequacy of the program in a city of 150,000 people with 10,000 to 12,000 out of work and only 143 being put to work? Can anyone seriously contend that the government responsible for that program has discharged its responsibility, particularly when it told the people of Canada, "No man or woman will ever be allowed to suffer, deficit or no deficit"? That is the situation. That was a solemn promise made to the people of Canada and we in his house cannot fail to remember that one man out of work means misery for a number of people in that family.
Difficult as this problem is for our society, we are not going to be able to escape our

responsibility in meeting what is a hard core problem of human misery in the case of those who have no work. Anyone who lives in a community like mine and knows something about this problem will realize why I feel so strongly when I discuss the problem, particularly in relation to a government that challenged the previous administration and said, "What they cannot do we will do".
I ask the Minister of Labour now to live up to that promise. Why will the minister not associate with this program the very suggestion, which he supported, made by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs when he suggested that we ought to have a parliamentary committee? May I ask the minister to listen to my question? Will the Minister of Labour direct his ears now to what I am saying? I am asking him a question.
He does not seem to be interested at all.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He was all ears a while ago.
I have asked three times now that the Minister of Labour listen to this question. [DOT]
I tried to ask the hon. member a question a while ago and he would not allow me to do so.

Will the Minister of Labour tell the house now why the administration of which he is a member will not take steps to establish a parliamentary committee so that we can examine the problem of unemployment?
The answer to that is that the hon. member for Essex East would use that committee for political propaganda.
Shame!

I am not going to answer that but I am going to put on Hansard what my hon. friend's colleague said on this very question in a debate in which he took part. The words are to be found at page 2083 of Hansard of 1953-54.
There is only one way in which parliament can get at the problem, and that is by setting up a special committee-and setting it up at once. We believe there should be such a committee, and that its first job should be to examine the unemployment situation and find out just exactly what the figures are. Either side may be wrong; perhaps the labour leaders are too high; the cabinet is probably much too low. But let members of the House of Commons find out for themselves what the actual unemployment situation in Canada today is. And, having done this, let them recommend to the house and the government the steps which could be taken to meet the situation, both the shortterm and the long-term problem. Let such a committee bring in worth-while recommendations which, I believe, would be of great help to the nation.
Supply-Labour
That was a statement made by the member who is now Secretary of State for External Affairs. He moved an amendment seconded by the Prime Minister, then the hon. member for Prince Albert, and the Minister of Labour spoke in that debate and supported the amendment which was an amendment to the motion to go into committee of supply. In view of the attitude taken by the minister and even if his last allegation was true, which of course it is not, how can he justify sitting in his seat day after day and ignoring suggestions that the recommendations which the hon. gentlemen have made should at least be attempted to be carried out by themselves now that they have the responsibility?
If my hon. friend does not accede to this suggestion, if he fails to adopt the other proposals which he has made, it is quite clear that he simply does not mean to try to tackle the problem of unemployment seriously. My hon. friend wants an example of the seriousness of the problem. I told him that last year 143 people were put to work in Windsor under this program. Compare that with this situation. The other day the civil service commission conducted a competition in that community for two customs and excise officers at a salary of $262.50 a month. The competition was held on January 23. Does my hon. friend realize that there were more people who applied for those positions than were put to work under my hon. friend's program to cure unemployment? Five hundred people sought the right to apply for these jobs, more than the number which my hon. friend's program put to work last year. But the story is not complete.
Ask the city council.

I always welcome the interjections of the hon. member for Edmonton West. My hon. friend says, "Ask the city council". That is what this government is now doing. It said, "Elect us and we will take care of the problem", but now that it has been elected it says, through one of its distinguished parliamentary secretaries, "Ask the city council". The people of Canada are asking this government.
The other day the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate made what I thought was a very constructive speech in which he suggested to the Minister of Labour that one way of taking care of this problem, by way of action supplementary to this particular program, would be to do more in the way of vocational training, and the minister, sitting in his seat and in his usual parliamentary manner, cried out, "That is what we are doing". I have no doubt that something is being done in the matter of vocational training but what is being done is as a result of

Supply-Labour
a program that was inaugurated long before the minister had the slightest expectancy of having a seat on the ministerial benches. It was brought in by the previous administration under the late Mr. Humphrey Mitchell and extended by Mr. Milton Gregg.
The minister has undoubtedly seen the report of the vocational training advisory council of his own department, a report that was referred to in a release made by the Department of Labour on December 8 and in which the chairman of the committee, Dr. McNally, pointed out that the study had indicated the rapidly increasing problem of unskilled workers in the labour force and the need for more vocational training. But then the minister still says that enough is being done. If he wants further convincing, I will ask him to read what the chairman of the unemployment insurance commission, now serving under the minister, had to say about this problem. He is reported in the Montreal Gazette of October 2 as saying that 8, 9 or 10 applicants had to be interviewed before a qualified worker could be found.
Does that indicate that the minister has taken steps to accelerate the training program so as to give men, for instance in Sydney and in other places, who have engaged in one form of occupation, an opportunity of developing skills which might assist them in solving the unemployment problem that confronts them. Mr. Bisson is reported as having said he studied this problem closely, and he went on to say he wondered whether it would not be better to train the unemployed at the very time when unemployment gives them the leisure to take advantage of the training. This was not a statement made two years ago, it was made last fall. And yet the minister said, by way of interjection to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, all that could or should be done was being done.
I say to the minister that the reluctance of the government to give any answers to the suggestions that have been made from this side of the house with regard to this problem, reveals either that the government is unaware of the severity of the problem or it does not feel capable of coping with it. This last situation would be an understandable one, but surely the Minister of Labour ought to tell this country whether or not he now feels, in the light of his experience, that it is possible for governments, individually at the federal level or the federal government and the provinces together, to do something about this problem. However, when the minister, the Prime Minister and all the others sit there and do not reply to questions put or to suggestions made that might be carried forward, then that constitutes an affront to

parliament and establishes clearly that this government is really not interested in doing something about this problem.

Are we only to have then from the Minister of Labour a continuation of this little program which last year put 33,000 to work and this year may put 40,000 to work or are we to have a real effort on the part of the administration to employ all of its power and its capacity to give work to men and women
