Mr. Chairman, this debate is somewhat limited by the terms of the estimate. I shall try to keep in order with my few remarks, but the question of unemployment is related to fiscal and trade policies, investment policy and general economic policy of the government. Of course, the terms of the estimate do not give us the opportunity to range into those fields very far.
However, before proceeding, I do think in all fairness we should express our appreciation of the thousands of Canadians who have done their best to co-operate with the do it now program. I know in the communities in my own district there are persons of modest means who have done what they could to co-operate with that program by providing work during the winter months in the way of repairs and minor construction jobs. I know of men of quite modest means who are providing a day's work a week for a man who is on unemployment insurance. I know individual persons who are having men cut their cordwood on the basis of a day's work a week. I think we should recognize that sense of responsibility on the part of those Canadians who have tried to do, in their small way, something to relieve the present situation.
I should like also to express my appreciation of those employers who have accepted some responsibility for the planning of their operations so that employment is provided, so far as possible, within the limits of this system and their own organization of work during the winter months. I am not one of those who is in the habit of looking upon all employers as questionable people because I have had the opportunity of sitting in with a number of employers, particularly in the lumber industry, who leave you to considerable expense to plan certain operations in the winter, and in many cases I am told they conducted these operations in the winter without a cent of profit. I mention that

because I think it is only fair to recognize that there are many employers and companies with a sense of responsibility to their fellow Canadians.
We in this group, as have other hon. members of the opposition, have criticized what we call this small piece of cake so far as the winter works program is concerned. We have criticized it because we considered it completely inadequate to meet the present situation. We think the government has failed to mobilize all those governments, agencies and persons in Canada who, with a sense of responsibility and good will, would be willing to co-operate with this government in a very much larger and much more effective plan.
There are several types of unemployment and several reasons for unemployment, even within that group of persons whom this winter works program is intended to serve. There are persons suffering unemployment for one of several reasons. We have cyclical unemployment, which is the worst form, caused by general trade and economic conditions. There are some who are suffering unemployment at the present time because of that condition. We have a certain amount of unemployment for personal reasons. These are all totalled up in the figures with respect to unemployment. The employer has disagreed with the employee or for family reasons, or for some other reason a man is out of work. I have known of a man to lay off work because his wife was going to have a child, and of course that is a personal reason. Then, there are others who want to change their occupation, and so on. We have regional unemployment caused by regional conditions and the disinclination or inability of those who are unemployed to go to another area. This may be the result of lack of funds to do so.
Then we have technological unemployment, which is increasingly serious in this country. I would say that is the nightmare of competition in the capitalist society. Then we have structural unemployment caused by the loss of markets or changes in consumer demand in certain industries where the industry itself is going out of existence. We have seasonal unemployment, too, which is largely occasioned by the weather. Many people are of the opinion that the winter works program is required because of seasonal unemployment, just to meet a certain amount of seasonal unemployment.
As I said before, we have persons unemployed in Canada because of one of the several reasons that I have mentioned. Without a doubt the present unemployment is caused by a combination of all of these factors and cannot be considered as purely a winter phenomenon. At the same time, 79951-0-65
Supply-Labour
we have to face the fact it is one of the elements in our changing capitalist society, one of the fruits of the system under which we live. It is for this reason we say that this program, whatever merit it has, is inadequate and does not take sufficient consideration of the long range point of view in the circumstances we face at the present.
I have given considerable thought to this and I am not one who blows off steam on a problem without giving some thought to it. In fact, I am one of those who thinks it is better to light a candle to lead even a Conservative government into the light, than to curse the darkness. I have discussed this matter with municipal officials and with employers; on occasion I have sat around the table with employers who accepted some sense of responsibility for unemployment. I have discussed it with employees, trade union officials, farmers and other people. I like to get people's ideas as to what can be done effectively to meet this type of situation. This is not a question that should be treated on a partisan or political basis. We are here as members of the parliament of Canada, as I see it, to try to express our views, to give our opinions and to advance suggestions in the hope that in the end our collective wisdom and our collective contributions will bear fruit in a program that will be effective and will meet the situation throughout the coming years.
I think there must be a general admission of the fact of the continuing nature of this malady by governments, by industry and by the public in general. In my opinion, there must be the will to plan with purpose to correct the unnecessary hardship caused by unemployment and to eliminate the unnecessary waste that is consequent upon that unemployment. I believe it is essential for the closest co-operation to be sought between federal, provincial and municipal governments, having in mind the thought that, regardless of our various points of view, we are going to work together to do something effective to meet this situation. That cooperation, as I believe the hon. member for Assiniboia implied or mentioned during his remarks, must be crystallized in the form of legislation. I believe we on this problem must get away from the bible of previous legislation. I am of the opinion that we must have some entirely new legislation to meet the changing circumstances of unemployment at the present time. But as I say, what is done must be based on legislation to meet the need.
Then I believe there must be a co-operative assessment of the problem and that provision must be made for providing reasonably adequate estimates of the number of unemployed

Supply-Labour
involved during certain periods. Then I think there should be a cataloguing of projects. Somebody mentioned a shelf of projects. In my opinion there should be a cataloguing of projects, such as house building, highway construction, road construction, the erection of public buildings and so on.
Another important factor is the timing of summer and winter projects in order to absorb the greatest number during the period of greatest need. For instance, during last summer we found a shortage of miners in certain areas-I refer to skilled rock men- and the mines were competing with one another for skilled miners while at the same time the government of the province was undertaking quite a heavy expenditure on high rock work where millions of dollars were being spent.
If there was a general spirit of co-operation between federal, provincial and municipal governments, having in mind the spending of public money to the best advantage, I think a committee or conference could arrange these matters so that they could say: we are not going to compete for labour when the miners are fully employed during the summer months; if we are going to have a total number of unemployed miners in British Columbia of, say 1,000 or 2,000, for instance, in the southern interior we are going to delay our work by agreement on these big rock bluffs until winter when the work can be done to better advantage than in the summer, and employ these men when they are unemployed in the winter. That is what I call a rational approach to the situation.
Then I think there must be co-operation between all concerned in the sharing of the cost. That will be done partly, no doubt, on the basis of contributions from taxation through the federal, provincial and municipal governments. But in addition to that, it may require some close co-operation with respect to providing particular municipalities with loans at a fairly low rate of interest, having in mind that the contribution made by the federal government will be repaid in effect by taking people off the unemployment insurance list, by preventing unnecessary social waste, by the income tax contributions that will be paid by those who are employed in this way or in other words by all those benefits that productive labour provides for the state.
Then I think we must give some serious consideration to modification of the Unemployment Insurance Act in order to stimulate initiative on the part of the employer and to reward initiative on the part of the employee. I might say at this point that I want to express my appreciation of men whom I have known-employees who were unemployed-who put themselves out to a

considerable extent, who were determined to find some employment if it was at all possible; and fortunately the majority of Canadians prefer to seek work rather than unemployment insurance.
Then I think some consideration must be given-and these things, in my opinion could all be considered by a joint committee-to modifications or changes in the Income Tax Act that will promote co-operation from the employers-the various companies and individual employers concerned-with a national policy or programs along the lines I have suggested in order to meet the continuing unemployment caused by the various reasons I have suggested.
Finally I think it is necessary for both federal and provincial governments to undertake a good public relations program in order to develop an understanding of the need, the policies and the required cooperation from all persons concerned in order to make it a success. In a democracy governments can organize from the top. They can spend money to meet a certain situation. But no program is thoroughly effective unless it has the co-operation of the people right across the country. That co-operation results from an understanding of what governments are trying to do. Every one of us has a personal responsibility to provide that understanding and to do what we can for the welfare of our fellow Canadians.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, that is all I am going to say at this time. I urge the government to mobilize the good will and the sense of responsibility of Canadians all across this country behind an effective program that will spring from federal, provincial and municipal co-operation in an effort to meet this problem of modern society in an effective and desirable manner.

Mr. Chairman, I know that, in 1958, many people were simple enough to believe that a saviour had arrived who would succeed in eradicating completely and finally the scourge of unemployment. I shall remind you of the statement made in Prince Albert, on February 14, 1958, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he said:
(Text):
As long as I am Prime Minister, no man or woman is going to suffer from unemployment so long as public works will provide them the assistance they require.
(Translation):
Yet, since that statement, we noticed that, far from improving, conditions are constantly deteriorating.
Some time ago, I was told that in the district of Ottawa-Hull alone-and I cannot quote

only the figures for Hull because they are integrated-there was in January an increase of 13,638 unemployed in the two municipalities. Now, as we know that the population of the city of Ottawa consists mainly of civil servants whose security at least with regard to employment, is assured, it can be inferred that the greater part of the unemployed are to be found in the industrial district, which is on the Quebec side.
Every day I meet people who come to me in order to complain and ask for help, after trying out public welfare organizations, or approaching the town hall and the St. Vincent society. In a word, they have come down to a state of virtual mendicity because the government did not find anything better than providing $15 million for winter works that are practically impossible to carry out.
The minister mentioned, a few moments ago, as he did the other day too, that there were nearly 800,000 unemployed in Canada, and that conditions are getting continually worse. Yet, we, on this side of the house, have been saying to the government since 1957: "Get ready, find the means, work out the plans, because unemployment is not going to decrease just now." And all we got as an answer was that there were more people working than ever before. As a matter of fact, the Prime Minister, when answering some questions himself, stated that it was quite possible that there should be at the same time more employment and more unemployment than in 1955, as a result of our increasing population, and prevailing conditions.
There may be more people employed than in 1955; but there is also an increased number of unemployed and that is the reason why we are asking this government to do something about it.
The government does not seem to do anything at all. They found a way this year, as they did last year, to make us vote an amount of $15 million to help the municipalities carry out winter projects and thus alleviate all the hardships resulting from unemployment.
What are we asked to do according to that scheme? We are asked to do this: to build and repair streets, sidewalks and roads, except highways.
We know that the only winter projects which can possibly be carried out are the extensive road work launched by governments when they decide to fill in pot-holes with rock in order to prepare the work to be done during the summer. But, in our municipalities, it is impossible to carry out 79951-0-65J
Supply-Labour
winter work in this way because, as the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Tardif) said, the ground is so deeply frozen that this kind of work will be very costly.
How could we, in Canada, build sidewalks in the winter months when we already have some difficulty in finishing such work in October and November? Indeed, the cement has to be covered up to stop it from freezing and breaking up afterwards. But all we are permitted to do is to build roads and sidewalks.
The laying of water mains is authorized; but we know that the installation of water mains during winter, though perhaps not impossible, is certainly extremely difficult because the frozen ground must be dug up before pipes are laid down on frozen soil, and there is great danger of the frost getting into the pipes and causing permanent damage.
The suggestion is made that we construct and develop parks in a country like Canada, where winter lasts from seven to eight months.
I consider that, considering the way winter works are prepared, it is nearly impossible for our municipalities to take advantage of them; and yet there is insistence that it be the sole program offered by the government to help the unemployed.
First of all, the amount is inadequate. The amount should be much larger, and the program itself should be prepared a long time in advance. In fact, at the present time, that is, in January, February and March, the government should give some indication of its intention about its unemployment program for next winter, so that municipalities might start planning their works and be ready to carry them out when the time comes.
Furthermore as the hon. member for Russell indicated, the assistance should not be limited to works of that type-which are impossible-but should extend over a much longer period, in order that municipalities might complete in the course of summer projects that were started in the wintertime. Municipalities would thus be induced to take an active part in this program.
Second, the type of works is limited. There are winter works that could be carried out in our municipalities and are not included there.
Apart from that, the government should consider the fact that the assistance provided under this program is limited.

Supply-Labour
$15 million which we are asked to vote as assistance to municipalities where there are unemployed people is insufficient, inadequate and ineffective.
That is why I submit that the burden of unemployment and of its hardships falls on the municipalities and the provinces. In fact, the municipalities are obliged to increase the cost of their welfare program considerably because this federal government which contended when it was in the opposition, that the unemployment problem was the responsibility of the federal government, does nothing to alleviate the burden of the municipalities.
Mr. Chairman, several members of this house claimed that the situation is worse now than when the Liberals were in power. Well, the figures given to us are either accurate or not so. If they are accurate, then the situation was better at that time; if they are inaccurate, this government should give us accurate figures. Here is what the Financial Post of November 1958 had to say:
(Text):
Bigger Load on Municipal Aid As Jobless Insurance Runs Out
(Translation):
This is what the Financial Post said. At the end of the item in question, we find the amounts paid by each province for public assistance purposes. I shall not quote the figures for all the provinces but only for those with the highest population.
In 1955-1956, the province of Quebec paid an amount of $3,103,000 to assist the unemployed; in 1958-1959, this amount reached $6,000,000, mind you, under a Conservative federal government. This means that public assistance costs have doubled in the province of Quebec; and still the present federal government takes no action and tells us that the recession has disappeared.
As for the province of Ontario, in 19551956, the provincial government had to pay $5,940,000 to help people out of jobs. In 1958-1959, the amount was doubled and reached $10,000,000. Now I understand why the Frost government is asking the present government for an additional amount of $100,000,000 to relieve the misery caused by the Conservative federal government.
Mr. Chairman, I could go on like this indefinitely and give examples that the government is not taking measures it was advocating at that time. I can hear members making ironical remarks. Those newcomers do not know what their present colleagues were

calling for when they were sitting on this side of the house, nor about the excessive language they used without being able to prove anything. Now that they are in power, they forget their past promises, they forget what they kept requiring of the former government. They merely let things slide, and do next to nothing to solve the hopeless financial situation they themselves brought about.
Mr. Chairman, we all know that there are people who are unemployed in winter. I believe that the government should increase the vocational training courses and, if necessary, compel the unemployed under thirty years of age who receive unemployment insurance benefit to attend classes two or three times a week to receive a training that would allow them to get a specialized trade and certain jobs which are offered at this time.
In fact, according to an item that has appeared in the Belfast Evening Telegraph, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration published a list of jobs available in Canada. We even offered to pay the transportation of those who would come to Canada. This advertisement appeared quite recently and those people were being asked to come to Canada because we need skilled workers. Here is the list of skilled workers we were inviting to Canada:

Accountants, aerodynamacist, architects, bakers and pastry-cooks; beauticians, bookkeepers, cashiers, bricklayers; butchers and meat cutters; cabinet makers; carpenters and joiners; cooks; dentists; dieticians; domestics; dry-cleaning and pressers; engineers; electrical; electronics; marine; farmers, general, dairy, livestock; farm workers; fitter, machinists; furniture upholsterers, hairdressers, ladies', gent's; hospital lab. technicians; housekeepers; librarians; machine tool setters; motor mechanic repairmen; nursemaids; nurses, professional and practical; occupational therapists, female; office machine operators; painters; physicians and surgeons; physiotherapists; plasterers; radio and t.v. mechanic repairmen; salesmen and shop assistants; sewing machine operators.

The federal government could contribute to that program through grants to the provinces, which would enable them to use their technical schools to train the unemployed to fill special positions.

I submit that this government and the Minister of Labour-

Mr. Chairman, at this time I should like to make a few brief remarks

on the item under discussion before the house. We are asked to approve an item of $15 million to provide payment to provinces in respect of Indian bands under the municipal winter works incentive program. It was stated this morning in the course of the debate that this was a step in the right direction on the part of the government. I agree that it is a step in the right direction but I must also add it is a most insignificant and inadequate step. It is so short a step that the government, even by its implementation, fails to reach the objective.
This morning the Minister of Labour released some figures showing the estimated expenditures by the provinces under this program. The total expenditure amounted to $83,900,000, of which the federal government will be called upon to pay a certain share. We were even told that the amount of $15 million may not be reached. When we look at the figures released this morning in connection with the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia-

I think I can clarify the situation. We have provided $15 million. We hope it is all claimed and we hope more is claimed. We are prepared to provide more if it is requested by the provinces and municipalities.

I certainly share the hope of the minister, but after what we have heard about the winter works program and the conditions which are imposed it is rather difficult to visualize that this figure will be exceeded. If, for example, we take the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, where projects have been approved totalling $1J million and where the federal government's share will be approximately $50,000, we can realize how limited the assistance will be. In fact, out of total expenditures of $83 million on such projects less than 3 per cent will apply to these provinces and the federal contribution to New Brunswick and Nova Scotia is less than three-quarters of one per cent of the cost of all projects.
How far will such a measure go in providing relief for the 33,000 unemployed registered at the unemployment insurance offices in Nova Scotia as at January 7 this year and the over 33,000 registered on the same date at the different offices in New Brunswick? How far will these projects go in providing even partial assistance-

Mr. Chairman, may I say to the hon. member that we are prepared to

-and they will provide practically no or very little assistance to the 6,000 unemployed in Gloucester county. This morning I ask the minister if he had received any representations from church groups in Pictou county asking for federal assistance to provide relief for the critical unemployment situation in that area. The Pictou county ministerial in special session with representatives of the Roman Catholic clergy, meeting in Westville on February 8, 1960, put forth the folowing resolution:
"That we deplore the present extremely serious unemployment situation existing in the county of Pictou and that we urge our governments to do everything possible to relieve this critical condition by taking immediate action in having a car order placed with the Eastern Car Company at Trenton, proceeding with public projects such as the federal building at New Glasgow, the trans-Canada highway, and such other projects for the benefit of our province and our dominion and for the employment of our people in Pictou county."
Further on in the article there is the following:
Father Chisholm said that men were willing to work but there was no work to be had.
The situation in Pictou county is just about similar to that existing in many other areas of the Atlantic provinces. I should like to know how many projects, for example, have been approved for the city of Saint John, New Brunswick, where, according to the figures released by the minister on February 3, 2,694 people seeking employment were registered at the unemployment insurance office, this notwithstanding the remarks made in the house last week by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert that unemployment was

no problem in his constituency. He is not concerned about almost 3,000 registered unemployed. The same thing applies to the 6,000 in Halifax, the 4,900 at New Glasgow, the 5,400 at Sydney and the 9,620 at Moncton and, as I have said, over 6,000 in my own constituency.
The Atlantic provinces, Mr. Chairman, need something worth while. As I have said before in the house, they need something going beyond the ordinary type of federal assistance to restore conditions to normal and to provide at least part-time employment to the substantial number of unemployed in these provinces. What we need now is a diversion from the northern vision of the government, a diversion directed toward the Atlantic provinces. Conditions in these areas will not be improved when we realize that for the present fiscal year public works projects will be reduced by almost $30 million.
What we need is a wider field of application of this program. We all agree that one of the main problems of the Atlantic provinces is transportation. The federal government should widen the field of application of this measure and extend special measures of assistance to the Atlantic provinces to build roads. Even if roads cannot be built properly during the winter months such measures could give employment at an early period in the fall so that those who cannot secure enough unemployment contributions to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits would at least have some measure of assistance during the winter months.
I know that many of these projects cannot be undertaken by the provinces alone. The minister mentioned a while ago that the federal government would be prepared to take into consideration further projects advanced by the municipality of Gloucester. I would bring to the attention of the minister the situation of the residents of Miscou island who need transportation to the island, who need a bridge. The bridge could be constructed either under the winter works program or under the roads to resources program in cooperation with the province of New Brunswick. This project could be carried on during the winter months and would provide employment to hundreds of residents of Gloucester county who, as I have said before, are deprived not only of unemployment insurance benefits but also of any assistance whatsoever from the province or the municipalities.
Therefore I feel it is the duty of the present government to extend the winter works program to make it applicable in such a way that it would be practical and would reach the objective for which it was introduced.

I might say also, Mr. Chairman, that since the present government-

Six thousand.

Six thousand, and I should like to ask my hon. friend how many are fishermen who for years and years in the past, not only were unemployed but did not get one dollar of assistance from the government.
There are 1,200.

This year the unemployed fishermen, these men who have always been unemployed all along our coast to the United States border, are being provided with unemployment insurance. My hon. friend knows that as well as I do. These are the facts and I am surprised at what the hon. member has said. As I say, it had not been my intention to take part in this debate this afternoon. However, when I know what the situation is in my own province I could not sit

idly in my seat and hear my hon. friend, for what purpose I do not know although I have a very good idea, stand up and place his own province in a position in which it should not be placed.
There has always been seasonal unemployment in our province. Let us take the example of the lumbermen in the woods, and we have many hundreds of them. During the winter months when there is snow on the ground these men work in the woods. As soon as the soft weather comes in the spring of the year, they have to come out from the woods and they become unemployed. There are no factories particularly in rural areas in which to put these men to work and they become unemployed. However, they receive unemployment insurance. My hon. friend knows about these situations, and they account for the names on the unemployed rolls.
I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that I could go through this Saint John Telegraph-Journal of February 9 again and show that there are many other undertakings which are going forward in the city of Saint John and in the province of New Brunswick. We are having and have had the greatest boom in the history of their city and in the history of our province and that only came about in the last two or three years since this Conservative government came into power and through the co-operation of the Conservative government under Hugh John Flemming in the province of New Brunswick.

I have a question of privilege. I have been accused by the minister, early in his remarks, of never getting up and speaking for my constituency when I was on the government side. I challenge the minister on that statement, and I challenge him to look at the record. If he does he will find that at least three or four times during every session when I was on the government side I spoke for the benefit of my constituency, which is more than any other government member from New Brunswick has done, including the minister himself, during the two years they have been in power.

I had not intended to intervene at this particular moment in this debate until we heard this regrettable speech by the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I would draw your attention to the fact, Mr. Chairman, that the minister was allowed to proceed along lines which members on this side were not allowed to follow. He talked about the general economic condition of New Brunswick; he talked about the development of Saint John and the development of Moncton.

I do hope that a similar latitude will be given, not just to me but to other hon. members on this side. I hope also that the Minister of Labour will find it possible to listen to what is being said in this committee instead of keeping up a constant babble of childish interruptions when other hon. members are speaking, which has characterized his conduct throughout this whole debate. This is not the way the minister is treated when he gets up to speak by the people on this side of the house.
It is about time these members on the other side of the chamber, who when they were over here talked so much about the rights of parliament, showed some little respect for them now that they are in positions of authority. I may say that goes particularly for the hon. member for Royal who is one of the senior members of the House of Commons. I will tell the hon. member for Royal that my friend the hon. member for Gloucester, who needs no defence of his conduct from any quarter in this chamber, is one of the best debaters in the House of Commons and is constantly talking about things that are before us and not about irrelevancies.
I want to tell the Minister of Veterans Affairs why the hon. member for Gloucester and everyone over here from the Atlantic provinces is concerned about the situation in the Atlantic provinces. The Minister of Labour said the other day on television that the recession was over. I am not going to argue-because it would be out of order- whether or not the recession is over. However, I am going to say this. In January of 1958-on January 20, as a matter of fact- the Prime Minister rose in his place in this chamber and told us that the government had at last discovered that there was a recession and they had discovered it from a dusty report. They had not realized it from the facts themselves. At the time the Prime Minister spoke in January 1958 there were 110,000 people on the rolls in the Atlantic provinces including fishermen. In January of 1960, when the Minister of Labour says the recession is over, there were in the same week- January 14, 1960-over 100,000 not including fishermen and the lowest figure for fishermen is 15,000.
When those two figures are added together, it means that there are at least 5,000 more people seeking work in the four Atlantic provinces today than there were two years ago at what the government called the depth of the recession. That is why we on this side of the chamber, notwithstanding the boom that has been produced in the Atlantic provinces by the speech of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, are concerned about an economic

condition in the Atlantic provinces which is worse than it has been at any time since the late war.
You do not know what you are talking about.

The hon. gentleman perhaps knows a great deal more about it than do the people there. But I can assure him that the 115,000 people, even including the fishermen who are unemployed and who would, in most cases, be very happy to have work to supplement their incomes in the winter months, as I know very well from the correspondence I get from the fishermen.
Then, of course, the rather shoddy effort of the Minister of Veterans Affairs to take credit to this government for unemployment insurance for fishermen was characteristic of the performance that we have had from this government on every question of this kind. When their deficiencies are pointed out they always say, "Well, the Liberals did no better" as if they had not promised to do things we did not do. But they were just promises. When anything good is referred to, they talk as though they had done it themselves, although invariably it was put on the statute books before they came into office, as was the case with unemployment insurance.
As I said the other evening, and that is why I wanted these figures and that is why I said the other evening we were entitled to have all these figures-
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Is it not true that our government put into effect in 1958 the Unemployment Insurance Act amendment extending further advantage in favour of the fishermen?

It does not happen to be true at all. The amendment to the act was made in the year 1957 and it became effective on April 1, 1957. The benefits were paid for the first time on December 1, 1957. The legislation was given royal assent when we were in office and the collection of the premiums began while we were in office. But it is true that, because of the date at which the act came into force, no benefits were paid or payable until after the present government came into office.
That is, of course, just exactly on a par with what the Prime Minister did in that broadcast on television when he talked about the previous government's neglect of social services generally and asserted or appeared to assert that this government was responsible for all those changes in the legislation 79951-0-66i
Supply-Labour
that Mr. Harris had made in his budget of 1957 which amounted to a more substantial sum than that which has been made available by the present government. This is characteristic, I say, of the kind of argument we have about this kind of thing.
But to return to the item before us, here are the figures the minister himself gave to the hon. member for Essex East. They appear at pages 707 and 708 of Hansard for February 3. These are figures showing the expenditures on this program in the year 1958-59: Newfoundland, $24,000; Prince Edward Island, $1,000; Nova Scotia, $337,000; New Brunswick, $234,000. If you add those figures together, you get about $600,000 out of the $6-J million or 10 per cent; that is to say, 10 per cent of the total federal expenditures on this program a year ago was expended in the Atlantic provinces.
In the Atlantic provinces, both a year ago and this year, I regret to say that one seventh of the unemployment in the whole country exists. It will therefore be seen very clearly that the point I made the other evening is perfectly correct, namely that that area which has the heaviest unemployment gets the least benefit from this program. That was the point the hon. member for Gloucester was making. He was making precisely that point. Why does the county of Gloucester not recommend more projects? The reason is that the county of Gloucester cannot afford to pay for them. That is the reason why. It is easy enough for the city of Toronto and perhaps for the newly rich city of Saint John, in the vision of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, to pay for them but we would be interested in knowing how many projects there are in Saint John.
There are 3,000 unemployed.

Exactly; there are 3,000 unemployed, as my hon. friend reminds me. In the village of Rockcliffe where I happen to live it would be very easy to employ all the unemployed on a very small project. We have not any projects because we have no unemployed. But in those areas where the unemployment is heavy and where the tax base is low and where the need is greater and where any government which took seriously what the Prime Minister promised would be done, would give the main application of this winter work program we get the least of it. The figures are even worse for this year.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Fisher (Port Arthur) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-16, to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1952, with respect to the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of the third presentation of this bill for discussion in this parliament it seems out of place to repeat all the arguments and data that were presented before, especially the first time the bill was presented in the house and discussed on June 12, 1958.
At that time I presented a bibliography on this problem and also circularized to all hon. members of the house statistics on the sizes of constituencies and their populations. There has as yet been no indication that the problem of redistribution has come much to the fore in the thinking of the government despite the fact that when the leading figures of this government were in opposition they had strong views on this subject which closely paralleled the objectives of this bill.
The purpose of this bill is to allow the setting up of some kind of commission independent of parliament to look after the redistribution following each census. As most hon. members are aware, at the end of every ten-year period when we have a census it is required under the British North America Act that there be a redistribution of the seats in this house in order that we can take care of the shifts and changes in population.
Shifts and changes in population are still going on and I know that each hon. member will be conscious of this to a greater or lesser degree. Personally I have been flabbergasted at the tremendous changes in my constituency just within the last three years. There has been an increase and that is not abnormal but the shift of population from one end of the constituency to another has been tremendous. I know this cannot be seen in constituency terms only in my area. It is going on in almost every part of Canada where there are fairly large metropolitan populations which magnetizes this shifting and magnifies the problem.
The other aspect of the question of redistribution that I wanted to highlight here is its relationship to the calling of an election. We are now in mid-term of this parliament and there are speculations about when the next election will take place. Redistribution greatly affects any decision in this regard. One of the distinguishing features

of our parliamentary set-up according to political scientists is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) or the government-we know in Canada it is the Prime Minister who will make the fateful decision-has authority at any time to ask the governor general to dissolve parliament and go to the people.
It has become a tradition to hold elections in Canada every four years or tending a little to the fifth year when the government has a large majority. Within a five-year period the Prime Minister has complete freedom of choice in this regard. As we all know, redistribution has to come constitutionally in 1962. The census figures will be available some time in March or early April of 1962 relating to the census of next year. Then there is a channel set up whereby the redistribution has to take place.
The present Prime Minister faces several difficult choices in this respect. If he goes to the people before redistribution is carried out he will be faced with the problem of having another parliament constituted for a four or five-year period on a basis of representation that is not fair and that will be 15 years out of date. Some of us may argue whether he should go to the people well before the end of his term when he has such a large majority, but that is neither here nor there. That is his prerogative, and he can go to the people. However, he and all those hon. members who support him will have to consider the factor I mentioned, whether they want another parliament to be constituted on the basis of this unfair, out of date representation.
I think that the Prime Minister with his respect for parliamentary institutions will have this problem to the forefront of his mind and it may be an important factor in determining when he calls an election. The year 1961 will bring the end of three full years of this government. I have heard speculation that there is likely to be an election next June. I discount this on the ground that I suspect the government would like to go to the electors after having introduced a much more radical legislative program than the one we have before us this session and in order to introduce a program of that kind it would require a considerable number of months next year. It occurs to me, therefore, we can only count on an election in the fall of 1961 at the earliest.
It seems to me that if the Prime Minister waits that long he is almost honour-bound to wait until we get the redistribution in 1962, and we cannot have a redistribution in 1962 and have an election before late August or September at the earliest. I make these remarks, Mr. Speaker, which some people may feel are beyond the point, to highlight the
British North America Act fact that this parliament right now should be considering-I will not be so presumptuous as to say this bill-this particular problem.
The more important hon. member for Halifax raised this in the debate on the speech from the throne; that is, he raised the issue in so far as-

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must apologize. I see some people are remarking at my singling out one member from Halifax as being more important than the other. I mean this in relation not to stature but just the fact that he is now the No. 2 man in Nova Scotia in so far as the government is concerned since he has been elevated to the important position of being the parliamentary secretary to the Postmaster General. He raised the issue here, Mr. Speaker, that the maritimes just did not want to face losing any seats. He did not seem to care particularly about Saskatchewan facing the loss of four, although perhaps he has some sympathetic feelings about it. But the point was that Nova Scotia did not want to loose another seat. If we do not do something very quickly, such as this bill tries to outline, or if we do not get into this whole question of redistribution soon, Nova Scotia may not lose a seat in the next redistribution, Saskatchewan may not lose four, Quebec may not lose one, Manitoba may not lose one, but we are going to have a parliament which follows a principle which does not really represent the population situation in Canada.
I feel that the Saskatchewan situation is close to the heart of the Prime Minister. After all, it is his home province. He would like to see those four seats saved. I know the picture which comes to our minds when we think of the kind of gerrymander which might take place, with every member from Saskatchewan being in the government party except the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue): I know the Prime Minister and the members from Saskatchewan-I can see a couple of benevolent one in the house here- would feel very badly about any inference that they would ever gang up on the hon. member for Assiniboia in redrawing constituency lines, or even gang up on themselves, because at least three of them would be disappearing from this house. I know they might want to concentrate upon the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) but I do not think we should raise this kind of possibility.
It seems to me this matter gives us a couple of alternatives. Should we increase the number of seats in this house so that there would be no more losses of this kind. Should

British North America Act we accept the principle from now on that no province will lose any more seats? I think this is worth very serious consideration. This would mean that we would have a constantly growing house as our population increases.
You all know some of the more ridiculous anomalies there are. Prince Edward Island has a population much below Scarborough but it has four members and Scarborough has only one. You can get the ridiculous comparison between Iles-de-la-Madeleine and Scarborough, or between some of the Montreal constituencies. One of the things that led me to introduce this bill is this. I looked at my friend from Timmins. He has a lovely little pocket borough, 35 miles by 35 miles. He can drive around it in an afternoon. He has a population half that of my constituency.
I was talking to a member from a constituency north of Toronto the other day. He was speaking about going home over the weekend and said that he had to drive 75 miles or 80 miles to interview some of his people. My situation, and the situation of people like the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Granger) or the hon. member for Saguenay (Mr. LaRue) or the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Hardie) is fantastic in comparison. The second largest group of polls in my constituency is 385 miles from where I live, and this is the kind of anomaly that we need to take into consideration.
This leads me to one of the principles that we need to introduce in our possible redistribution. First of all, we need to consider the principle that no province shall lose any more seats; second, we need to consider the fact that the old idea of there being two kinds of constituencies in Canada, rural and urban, is no longer valid. I think we have at least four different kinds; we have the metropolitan constituencies in highly urbanized areas such as Trinity. Then, we have the suburban type of constituency such as York West or Scarborough. Then, we have what I may call the proper rural constituency, or the real rural constituency, such as you have in most of the prairies or in rural Ontario, represented by people like the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe).
Then, you have what to me is the most difficult of all constituencies, and this is what I think of as the frontier constituency. There are quite a host of them. If hon. members care to look at the areas of constituencies in square miles they will find that there are over 30 of them that have more than 11,000 square miles. Some of them are fantastically large. You could tuck all the maritime provinces into my constituency, and you can do the same in Churchill and in a few of the others.


I would suggest that one of the things we need to do in this parliament-and do fairly soon, perhaps in the committee on elections- is to work out some principles that we can apply to redistribution, to face up to the complaints that are coming from the mari-times and Saskatchewan about losing seats. It seems to me the only way we can do this is by appointing something like an independent commission, after we give them the principles under which they work.
I have already mentioned in this house that I dislike seeing the prerogatives of this house diminished by the creation of boards and commissions; but I think our past history in this particular regard points out the need for a commission and I hope that hon. members know that I am painting this lily as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the Prime Minister did when they were talking on this subject in past parliaments.
I think we need an independent commission because of the very complexities of drawing boundaries. I suggest that on the commission we need a geographer, a demographer, a jurist, and then someone who has some experience in political life. I know it is going to cost a certain amount, but it seems to me it is necessary to guarantee to people what we really want basically from our electoral system, namely that each Canadian's vote is roughly, within some degree of tolerance, equal in value.
I can even get an argument boiling up in Fort William and Port Arthur. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) is elected with quite a few fewer votes than I am, 'and when I point out to my constituents that their votes are not worth as much as that of the voters in Fort William they can readily see it in terms of this question and get quite wrathy about it. Actually there are much greater paradoxes than that particular difference. I think all hon. members would like to see this worked out.
There is one special problem in connection with redistribution that has to do with this question of provinces losing seats that we must consider, namely the attitude of the French Canadians, and the attitude within that general attitude of Quebec province herself. I would suggest that those of you who are interested in this should read the Tremblay report and those sections of it which deal with this question. There is a very strong attitude in Quebec, as outlined in a letter I received today, that in so far as their representation in this house is concerned they feel it should be a matter decided on a provincial basis.
I myself find this repugnant. I think it is contrary to the whole concept of Canada, but

this is another attitude we have to consider. This was expressed very forcibly in this house two years ago by a couple of the members from Quebec, namely the attitude that representation within this house is in many ways a provincial matter and that no changes should be made in it; that no developments should go along this path unless the provinces are consulted. This is a difficulty in the way of working out a solution but I think it should still be approached.
One viewpoint I must comment on, because it was expressed by a prominent Canadian, was that put forward by Premier Frost in relation to the malapportionment of constituencies in Ontario. He said that he felt very strongly that the rural constituencies should be much smaller in population than urban constituencies. He did not make this point on the basis of the old argument that used to be popular that there were certain sturdy yeoman characteristics amongst rural folk that made them more perceptive and more able to appreciate political problems. Rather, he made it on the basis that the city people did not have to worry particularly about their protection from government through having representation. They had the newspapers to represent them and take up matters for them.
This is a most interesting idea to have injected into this particular kind of discussion and I do not think it can be taken too seriously. Yet perhaps it is a factor that any committee of the house or any group should investigate.

I think that has to be the ideal. Of course it is an ideal you are never going to attain because population shifts are always taking place. But the median in the next redistribution is going to be somewhere between 64,000 and 66,000 people. Every member knows how many people he has in his constituency and he knows how far he is from the median. But I do not think it is defensible. Many of my relatives, for example, live in the constituency of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe and I know that their votes are not worth five times the votes of the people in my constituency. It just is not so. We have got to try to move toward the median and the norm, and in a country like Canada this means change all the time.

We have had no indication at all from the government on how they are going to handle this problem. It seems to me that the hidden persuader in the whole deal is the Saskatchewan loss of four seats. I hope this hidden persuader is functioning right at the present time to induce the government to consider a rational approach to the redistribution problem. I make no claims for the bill I have introduced as being the final solution but I think what it does attempt to do is to make us see the problem in terms of a set of principles to give an independent commission which is the only way we will get out of what can be a great jackpot in 1962.
I have heard some fearsome stories from members of all parties and from some who are no longer here about what takes place when there is a redistribution. Evidently you break up into provincial committees and within the provincial committee you try to strike your bargain. You push some voters here and you pull some there. One of the points that is most obvious if we go along with this kind of system is that it will be mostly a case of Conservatives pushing Conservatives. This will be very true on the prairies, to a certain extent in British Columbia and completely in Nova Scotia. Where the real battles will be joined will be in Quebec and I imagine that particular provincial committee will be very late in reporting unless we do something beforehand.

If there is no action there will be the recrimination that I think is most justified, namely that the Prime Minister would let the people vote in another election upon a basis that constitutionally and simply as a matter of fairness is 15 years out of date. For that reason I should like to see the bill passed or sent to a committee. I would much prefer that than to have it talked out with either amiable or irritable irrelevancies.

I notice that the hon. member in this particular presentation as in previous presentations has made the point that no province should lose any seats. He also said some time ago, as found on page 1092 of Hansard for June 12, 1958:
You begin to get development of the idea that the rural voter is worth more than the urban voter.
His whole point, of course, is representation by population and that every voter shall have an equal vote in terms of value from the standpoint of the election of members. If we were to take this proposition and apply it to Prince Edward Island with a population of roughly 110,000, the House of Commons after the next election would have around 600 members, and just the very thought of 600 members-

He has pointed out the complexity of urban ridings and, presumably, the simplicity of rural ridings. I come from an urban riding but I consider that each of my electors has not got just one member but that the city of Vancouver has six members. In the hon. member's group there is the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), and I think it will be noticed that if the interests of the city of Vancouver are scratched then no one member but all members from that city are scratched, and that applies a great deal to the province as well.
But that is not true of the rural ridings. I am indebted to the hon. member for the bibliography that was included in his speech on June 12 last which gives a list of references. I should like to refer to one reference in that list, the "Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science", volume 15, 1949. I do not wish to quote very much from this publication but I think this passage on page 489 is pertinent to our discussion:
When the delegation, of Canadian statesmen who negotiated the final drafts of the British North


America Act reached London in 1866, their first outline of the confederation bill contained the following note about constituencies: "The readjustment to be made by an independent authority, as some of the judges, to be specified in the Imperial Act."
Later, on the same page, it goes on to tell about the great gerrymandering of the later years, in 1872 and 1882, and how that was conducted as well as how the present system evolved. The present system, as all hon. members know, is a committee of parliament. However, as this work goes on to say, it is not just a committee of parliament but it is rather a conference of the parties. In order that every province and every party may have a voice in its proceedings, the committee has grown so large that the last few redistributions have been effected by subcommittees, one of which is set up for each region or province. Neither the committee nor the subcommittees meet in public, nor is any record kept of deliberations; but there can be little doubt that proceedings are sometimes rather boisterous, for members have referred in the House of Commons to such committee activities as maps torn up, threats and invitations to mortal combat. This book goes on to talk about one member who complained because there were three members from his province, one from each of the three parties, and it was a question as to which two parties could gang up on the other one.
The philosophy behind this bill is one which I think would appeal to everybody. I do not think gerrymandering is anything to be concerned about today. I do not think it could be of value, and I think it could react against the party that was trying to do it. An example of this was cited in the case of	the	present Prime	Minister	(Mr. Diefenbaker) when his riding of Lake Centre was eliminated, and it did not seem to stop the Prime Minister from winning elections. I was very interested in what the hon. member had to say about that. On page 1094 of Hansard	the	hon. member	said that	the
Prime Minister had his riding not only gerrymandered but eliminated. However, this circumstance only made the Prime Minister determined to seek and win another seat. I think that is another one of the remarks of the hon. member with which I can agree.
The hon. member has made some point out of the fact that this is midterm, so to speak, and that the election perhaps would normally take place in	1962. By law	the redistribution can	only	take place after a census	and
there would not be time to go through the necessary procedures in order to get redistribution effected unless the election were late in 1962. I wonder how this particular authority would do any better? They cannot start working on this problem until after

the figures are in from the census people. This body would necessarily be limited in size and they would have the problem of studying every riding in every province throughout Canada in order to come to some sort of a fair arrangement. Even then, no matter how well they do their job or how long they spend on it, we will not reach that stage of perfection that the hon. member would like to see, that is each vote having an equal weight. I believe that is something that is simply impossible to achieve.
I am quite convinced that the job done by the committees in the past, with the odd exception and there are odd exceptions, has not been too bad. Perhaps a judicial committee-perhaps it might not be a judicial committee because the hon. member has outlined how it would be constituted

might do a better job in some ways, but it might do a worse job in others. I noticed that in presenting the bill in the session to which I was referring the hon. member said that he hoped everyone would take a non-partisan stand because that is the essence of redistribution. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Chambers) was the final speaker in that debate and he mentioned that he thought this was the way this committee was working. -he will find in evidence the mood that has been expressed in the speeches we have heard tonight- one of give and take and fair play for all concerned-and it is possible that a commission, better defined than that proposed in this bill, will be established.
Then, the hon. member for Port Arthur said, "How naive can you be?" When the hon. member says we should enter this debate in a non-partisan spirit, he should not tell us we are not capable of entering such a discussion in a non-partisan way. Frankly, so far as my own riding is concerned, I would be willing to leave it to any committee or any body to make any changes they wished in that riding because I am quite convinced you cannot manufacture an advantage through changing the boundaries of your riding, particularly a city riding. Perhaps in some rural areas it may be so, I do not know.
I believe, therefore, that the philosophy behind the bill is something for which we should work and I could support the spirit in this bill. I cannot support some of the reasons the hon. member has given for this bill or some of the ways he thinks it should

He referred to Timmins being half the size of Port Arthur. I was checking on a few things myself, but my calculations were based on electors not on population. After all, you are really trying to equalize the value of the votes, so you are trying to equalize the electors. That is quite true; the hon. member did state that the second largest group of polls was some 380 miles away from where he lives, whereas to cross Timmins was only about 30 miles. I do not know if the figures are right, but it is in that area. The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson) represents 32,474 electors and the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Cadieu) represents 17,704 but the Meadow Lake constituency is as large as the maritime provinces put together. A great deal of that is just an area on the map, and there is nobody there, but at the same time there are problems within that riding which are such that that area must have representation.
You do not, therefore, come down to any clear-cut, easily found solution to a problem like this. There are many different variances, and there may be some voters in some areas of Canada whose votes will have a higher value than those of other areas. What about the electors in Mackenzie River or in Yukon? There are 6,071 in Yukon and 6,716 in Mackenzie River. The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) told us that all the residents in the Northwest Territories do not have a vote. This bill does not even cover all of the Northwest Territories. Hence I think that the hon. member has fallen into the pitfall that seems to be inherent in so many bills which are brought in by members of his party. On the face of them the bills make sense

British North America Act and they are worthy of support but they over-simplify the problems which face us not only in areas of economics, social justice and the rest but in this particular area, the area of politics.
I do not think the present system should be condemned to the extent the hon. member has intimated that it could be condemned. At the same time, as I said when I started out, I do not like the principle behind this bill with regard to an independent body. I do not like the phrase "independent of the parliament of Canada." The hon. member has qualified that in that we should set up the principles which should govern that body. The very fact that it is an independent body and yet be permitted to say-this commission or whatever we may call it-how the people shall elect the members to this house is something on which I would require to have much more information before I could agree to it.
The only thing I do say is this. It is like divorce bills. If we could get rid of them, everybody would be happy. If we could get rid of this responsibility and could have as good a job done as has been done-except for the odd exception which has taken place in the last little while and which were common in the late 1800's and the early 1900's- then I would be prepared to go along with this bill. But at the present time I feel that our system is not too bad.
As I said before, it is not really a committee of the house; it is a conference of parties. I doubt whether any member of the C.C.F. party or of the Liberal party would allow any member of the Conservative party to get away with one thing with regard to changing boundaries which would mitigate against his chances of being elected. I think it is in that free interplay between the parties that honesty and perhaps the fairest type of redistribution is achieved.

Mr. Speaker,
I would just like to add a few remarks to those of the hon. members who spoke before me on the bill under review.
I want to start by summing up what I said last year on the matter.
I think it was mentioned a few moments ago that it would be well to proceed with the redistribution of ridings across Canada by having a more adequate urban representation or even by giving consideration to the areas where the urban population is more numerous.

I also believe, as I said last year, that the territories with huge natural wealth should be adequately represented in this house. As the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) said recently, it is true that those areas are sparsely populated or for the most part not settled at all, or even as they have often been called, just some area on a map.
It is also true that the greater part of those areas contain huge wealth and undeveloped natural resources and that they have as much right to be represented in this house as the more densely populated cities.
When the matter was discussed last year, I mentioned that since confederation, that is, since 1867, and up to 1952 there had been modifications in various constituencies according to an increase or decrease in population here and there across the country, and that there were barely 37 ridings that had not been affected by such changes.
This proves, I think, Mr. Speaker, that the committee, which sat on various occasions in order to study redistribution, did the job assigned to it as the necessity arose.
And apart from a few triflng exceptions, referred to a moment ago by the hon. member for Vancouver South, particularly the suppression of the constituency of Lake Centre -as we all know-apart, as I say, from a few trifling exceptions, redistribution was carried out generally to the best knowledge of committee members and with the greatest possible consideration for the Canadian people as a whole.
Now, I should like to refer to some remarks made a moment ago by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), when his bill was introduced. He referred, among other things, to the view expressed by members from the province of Quebec, who were aware of the Tremblay commission report, that is, the provincial commission appointed to consider constitutional matters concerning the province of Quebec in particular.
I would like to point out some of those remarks which seem to come much nearer the view expressed, last year, by that same member in this house. This quotation concerns the hon. members for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm and for Berthier-Mas-kinonge-Delanaudiere (Messrs. Pigeon and Paul).
Here is what Mr. Fisher said, as recorded on page 3729 of Hansard:
I seem to have forgotten the hon. member for Joliette-L/Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) who, along with the hon. member for Berthier-Maski-

nonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul), concentrated on an argument which is very familiar to anyone who has watched the Quebec scene. In my opinion, the source of their argument can be found in the Tremblay report, in which the line of argument is strongly adopted that redistribution concerns one part of the British North America Act that requires provincial consultation. As a matter of fact, I think the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm adopted exactly the idea that is in the Tremblay report, that once the bases have been determined for general provincial representation, the whole problem should be handled by the province itself rather than the House of Commons. In my view this is an indefensible position, in that the House of Commons must continue to hold the right to set up, for example, this independent commission, and if the independent commission does not work, to make any other amendment or change that is necessary.
The hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere was generally in favour of the idea of putting redistribution under a commission, but he did want this exception, that the commission should be determined on a provincial basis and the provincial authorities should enter into it.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member told us a moment ago that the problem would have to be faced, despite the problems raised by hon. members from the province of Quebec. I would point out to him that under the constitution, if there is to be no increase in the number of seats, it would seem, in my humble view, that the house could have a committee look into the matter of redistributing the constituencies, as has been done in the past. I think we might let each province keep the same number of members. At that time, I think we would have to seek the consent of the provinces. I am no expert in this field, but I sincerely believe that under the constitution, the provinces have the same rights as the federal government when a major amendment is proposed; in any case, such proposals are almost invariably referred to the provinces, as in the case of the resolution put forward by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) with regard to the term of office of judges, a resolution which is now on the order paper and should be passed shortly. I also understand that this amendment has been referred to provincial governments.
The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), raised another point when he mentioned in his bill that the matter could only be decided by an independent commission. I am inclined to share the view of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Chambers), which was placed before the house last year by the hon. member for Port Arthur, on page 3730 of Hansard:
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George brought up a legal point as to whether or not the words ''independent commission" were really valid
British North America Act
because of the fact that parliament would always have the right to change a decision made some years ago about this section, and to change it or alter it at any time. In other words, you may set up an independent commission but it would not be there in perpetuity, so therefore it would not be an independent commission.
In other words, the question of the definition of the word "independent" is purely academic. Parliament always has control over a commission appointed by it. I feel that no commission should be completely independent since it is appointed by the people's representatives, and if those representatives do anything wrong they will be blamed for it and will be answerable for it to their constituents.
Before concluding my remarks, I would like to make a suggestion in line perhaps with the proposals on the whole of the hon. member for Port Arthur, or which would meet with his approval.
I believe that the house already has the authority to create a parliamentary committee which, in the past, has studied this question of the representation, after each census. As the next census will be taken in 1961, the hon. member for Port Arthur seems to believe that it will be completed in time for the next general election, that is by the month of March. Should the next census be completed by the month of March, he thinks that the next election would take place before 1962. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South. However, on that matter, may I make other suggestions to the hon. member for Port Arthur. Since the creation of a commission or a committee is generally accepted, it seems to me that we should rather form a special commission which would be asked to study this question in the light of the result of the 1961 census. Besides that committee or special commission could be formed by the federal government in cooperation with the governments of the ten provinces. In any case, the ten provinces will have to agree unanimously to any amendment which would tend to change the present provisions of the British North America Act.
The commission could even do more than a simple redistribution, according to the movement of the population. It could be authorized to study the advisability of increasing the number of seats in the Canadian parliament, because of the increase of the population of Canada in general, especially since the last world war.

British North America Act
Mr. Speaker, an increased number of seats in the House of Commons would also allow more adequate representation for certain of the larger cities and especially for important parts of our country where major developments will be taking place in the future, even if the population of those areas is not as large, being scattered over a vast territory, as in the case of my own constituency and of several other large ridings in Canada where the population is also scattered.
Because of the promising future of Canada and of its ever increasing population, it seems to me that the time has come to increase the number of members.
This committee could look over the situation in order to submit a report before the next general election, so that each province may at least keep the same number of members as at present.

1.	Has any agreement been concluded between the governments of Canada and the United Kingdom in the matter of reciprocal arrangements regarding social security benefits?
2.	If so, was such an arrangement first presented to parliament for discussion and consideration? If not, for what reason?
3.	What is the significance, if any, of correspondence exchanged in the matter of social security benefits between the governments of Canada and the United Kingdom, as recently tabled?
Answer by: Hon. J. W. Monleith (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
1.	The provision of social security benefits under Canadian and United Kingdom laws to persons making application for benefit in one country who have resided for a period of time in the other country has been the subject of an exchange of correspondence between the United Kingdom high commissioner to Canada and the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The details of the arrangements made are set out in the correspondence which was tabled in the house on January 22, 1960.
2.	Reference to the aforementioned correspondence will make it clear that no new responsibilities in respect of social security have been assumed by Canada which would require any change in existing legislation; nor will any benefit payments be made to persons under Canadian laws as a result of the arrangements made in this correspondence which are not already authorized under the existing laws. While there was, in consequence, no necessity to refer this matter to parliament, nor to seek parliamentary authority for any legislative change, copies of the correspondence containing full details of the

arrangements that have been worked out were tabled as soon as possible after the opening of parliament.
3.	By arrangements set out in that correspondence, it will now be possible for persons in the United Kingdom, formerly resident in Canada, to qualify, subject to certain conditions, for United Kingdom family allowances, retirement pension and unemployment benefit by virtue of their previous residence or employment in Canada.
After making a detailed study of the residence and other conditions of eligibility contained in Canadian legislation (respecting family allowances, old age security, old age assistance, blindness and disability allow-
Questions
ances, unemployment insurance and hospital insurance), the United Kingdom authorities came to the conclusion that, without any changes in the Canadian laws as presently constituted, they would be justified in relaxing certain of the requirements of their own legislation in favour of persons coming or returning to the United Kingdom with earlier periods of residence in Canada. The Canadian government for its part has undertaken that it will keep the United Kingdom advised of any changes which may be made by parliament from time to time affecting the position under Canada's social welfare laws of persons from other countries who come to settle in Canada.
